This study provides a comprehensive classification of constant curvature metrics on the sphere with conical singularities, featuring a unique, canonical representation. We also investigate the existence of such metrics with a specific curvature value, and discover that a certain condition on the weights of the conical singularities leads to a complete and orientable surface. Furthermore, an explicit formula is derived for the Schrödinger operator's spectral parameter dependence in the case of two conical singularities, which generalizes previous findings by Rosenthal and Buckhurst. This research is presented in the context of recent results from related studies.

To understand the forces driving its motion, researchers created a model of a centipede, which moves through a viscous fluid environment, leaving behind a moving boundary wave. To simulate this behavior, computational models were developed to study two scenarios: a pinwheel model with no fluid memory and a model incorporating fluid inertia and a memory effect modeled using the popular Boussinesq approximation. To calculate the drag exerted by the wave on the centipede, researchers integrated the drag equation, taking into account both the velocity of the wave and its rate of change, into a dynamic model. These models were then applied to a hypothetical centipede, which moves by peristalsis - contracting and relaxing its body segments. To achieve forward motion, three of its body segments need to oscillate in sync; if more segments oscillate, the centipede moves faster. To determine the minimum number of oscillating segments needed, researchers applied mathematical constraints, taking into account the centipede speed, body size, and the drag equation, to establish a relationship between its size and the minimum number of oscillating segments. This mathematical approach revealed that, while fluid inertia and fluid memory have similar effects, they exert a weaker influence on the centipede's motion compared to fluid wave drag.

A proposed methodology called adaptive simulation will link bottom-to-top ocean models with top-down shoreline models through a flexible data integration approach that efficiently manages the diverse time and space requirements of each model type. This methodology will bridge the gap between deep ocean and shoreline scales, potentially increasing output resolution by up to 25 times, thus enhancing tsunami inundation modeling capabilities.

Detecting massive galaxies beyond redshift of 3 is crucial for completing the cosmic census during the reionization epoch because they are among the largest structures that existed during this time.  A recent study using data from the Spitzer-ERS and the Infrared Science Archive found 129 candidate galaxies at redshifts ranging from 5.3 to 7.0.  These candidates were identified through deep infrared searches, and further analysis using spectroscopy could confirm their identities would be a significant step forward in understanding the evolution of galaxies during this time.  However, spectroscopy using current telescopes is beyond their capabilities, and therefore candidates identified through photometric methods are relied upon.  However, relying solely on photometric methods can be problematic as they often fail to account for the complexity of the galaxies' light outputs, and therefore may misinterpret redshift for magnitude.  A proposed next step would be to use algorithms that can better account for this effect to improve the accuracy of photometric redshifts, and thereby their corresponding estimates of galaxies' physical properties.

We introduce a seven-dimensional gravity framework, which can yield the warped Adbl space and three-subspaces based on the Poincaré space, as well as obtain Killing spacetimes with Killing horizons. Additionally, by incorporating extra dimensions, we can also access the Adbl space and form a black hole solution with a non-zero cosmological constant. Furthermore, this framework offers a new method to investigate seven-dimensional gravity.

In a study on disk jamming, we analyzed the packing of closely spaced disks within a rectangular channel, confined to move only horizontally, similar to a multi-directional autonomous guided vehicle's cargo hold. Utilizing a genetic algorithm to attain optimal, densely packed configurations, our research examined how lateral disk movement influences their arrangement. Unpredictably, our results indicated that heavier disks exhibited the highest packing densities. These dense configurations provided the rigidest structure when subjected to lateral tension, compared to unloaded disks. Additionally, for all examined widths relative to the channel's length, this tension resulted in significant disk movement, an effect that persisted when compared to regular binary mixtures of spherical beads. Ultimately, this study offers insights into autonomous vehicle cargo storage.

Research suggests that three distinct types of El Ni\~no (warm phase of the El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation) and La Ni\~na (cool phase of the El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation) exhibit varying precipitation trends. We investigate how these different types' precipitation effects differ by employing machine learning methods to reduce the complexity of the Global Precipitation Climate Data Archive from 3200 to 128. We analyze the spatial information in these reduced components to investigate the types' precipitation patterns. We also develop a novel statistical test to identify extreme precipitation events and assess whether each type of El Ni\~na/La Ni\~na has unique characteristics using a non-parametric approach. Our findings reveal that each type of precipitation event has distinct characteristics, which are valid for both 1981-2016 and in a bootstrapped sample of 1035 years. Furthermore, we identify that the types of El Ni\~na/Southern Oscillation have distinct precipitation trends in specific regions, which could influence food security, water management, and human well-being in areas such as Africa, South America, and Southeast Asia.

Nonaffine behavior within the elastic range of soft materials has become the subject of renewed interest. Initially dismissed due to the presence of inherent defects in materials, like entanglements or cross-links, in this regime; instead it can now be included. The possibility of nonaffinity emerging in the elastic regime of soft materials is now a possibility. The presence of nonaffinity can be confirmed through a simple test, invovling a comparison of the material's affine and nonaffine linear moduli, which in fact are equal in the case of nonaffine models. The team conducted an experiment using 3D printing technology and technologically advanced 3D printed fibrils made out of polybutadiene to measure the linear elastic constants of a material with a microdouble network structure. In doing this, they discovered a point, marked by a discontinuity, where the stretching behavior of the material transitions from slow to fast stretching. The team found that this transition point coincides with the point where the stretching behavior of the individual polymer chains within the material switch from slow to fast stretching. The team's results confirm that even within the elastic range of this material, the stretching behavior of the individual polymer chains exhibits nonaffine behavior. The team has further suggested the presence of nonaffinity in soft materials by pointing out that it may manifest as an 'elastic critical point', an idea supported by both simulations and experiments conducted on a number of different materials.

This paper explores the existence of multiple population models that involve stochastic processes based on earlier single population models described by Cushing. Cushing found that these single population models had solutions that did not fit the long-term behavior predicted by them due to an unstable equilibrium. Multiple population models considered here include models with a dependent relationship between the populations, a model that reaches an unstable equilibrium, and a model that remains positive over time. Cushing found that the models that do not fit the long-term behavior predicted by them have solutions that do fit for the multiple population models that remain positive over time but not for the models that do not fit the long-term behavior predicted by them.

This study examines the computational difficulty of finite model finding for fuzzy logic models combining language constraints (fMTL), a framework that incorporates fuzzy logic operators into PNL with the until and diamond operators. We investigate whether there's an algorithm that can determine if a finite fuzzy logic model combining language constraints can match a given syntax-defined formula. Our research reveals the tractability of the problem for a fragment of fMTL with language constraints and path constraints but becomes NP-complete when we consider additional operators like bounded until-and-dafter. In a surprising turn of events, it also turns out that adding the everywhere operator makes the problem complete for NP.

Taxonomy expansion is a process of automatically adding subcategories to an initially selected category, guided by user-defined criteria. The expanded taxonomy is then presented to the user for review and confirmation. The existing techniques for achieving this purpose rely on either rule-based systems or neighborhood-based algorithms, both of which have their limitations. The former requires a meticulous definition of rules and is susceptible to shortcomings, while the latter struggles with efficiently handling data that has an uneven subtaxonomy balance. This research presents a new approach, the HyperExpan algorithm, which addresses these issues by providing a more effective solution for taxonomy expansion. The proposed method is known as HyperExpan, and it stands out from previous algorithms by incorporating two key features: a hyperparameterized model that accounts for geometric relationships within data and the ability to perform predictions with both accuracy and efficiency. The performance of the HyperExpan algorithm has been compared with other techniques for taxonomy expansion, with the results indicating substantial improvements in accuracy and faster processing speed, occurring in conjunction with stable hyperparameter values.

Quantum Chemical Predecessor Methods have been further developed using density functional approximations, which employ previously established quantum chemical post-processes to forecast molecular electric properties. The accuracy of eight DFT-based approximations in predicting various properties, such as dipole moments, dipolar polarizabilities, and anisotropy, was evaluated for 19 molecules through a comprehensive benchmark study involving 377 dimers. The outcomes showed that approximations based on DFT value or estimated values for individual atoms and bonds yielded less precise results compared to those using total DFT properties. The approximations' predictive performance was notably influenced by the method's underlying DFT calculation, where certain DFT methods produced better results than others. Notably, the B3LYP/6-31GG* DFT method produced the lowest root-mean-square error for total properties, while B3LYP/TZ2P basis set yielded the lowest error for property components. The outcomes also indicated that errors in predicting electric properties are largely independent of the molecular dimer's orientation. The established QChem Predecessor Methods have great potential for applying fast and approximate DFT methods, such as those using DFTB/Empirical long-range DFT/On-the-fly potential surfaces to accurately and efficiently predict electric properties of large systems.

Quantifying system performance under uncertain parameters is vital for complex industrial systems. However, practical constraints such as limited and often uncertain model data, high-dimensional performance dependencies, and restricted computational resources hinder the use of traditional Bayesian methods for systems modeling. To address these issues, a novel approach is presented that employs Monte Carlo randomized algorithms combined with belief propagation for efficient and accurate uncertainty modeling in discrete-time nonlinear systems. By leveraging modern hardware, this method can efficiently calculate the probability distribution of system states given uncertain parameters. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated on a hybrid system with extensive non-deterministic uncertainty in both continuous and discrete states. Compared to traditional Monte Carlo methods, the proposed approach reduces computational complexity and achieves comparable state estimation accuracy.

Quantifying an system's ability to function during failures has traditionally focused on overall system performance. However, prior efforts have neglected the importance of specific system features and their respective goals. This paper proposes a method for evaluating critical systems based on their advanced specifications, which incorporate multiple functional and non-functional aspects. Such detailed specifications enable the measurement of a system's capacity to meet its objectives in the event of component malfunctions. The Resilience Satisfaction Value (ReSV) function assesses the degree to which a system's specifications are met under failure conditions, enabling comparisons with baseline systems that have undergone upgrades to enhance their resilience. The ReSV function prioritizes key system attributes and their respective timing constraints when calculating a system's satisfaction level. The paper provides specific examples to illustrate the ReSV concept and its application, focusing on scenarios where failure impacts system performance differently, influencing the evaluation process.
Dark matter research is a prolific area with multiple approaches being explored.

We examine the nonlinear diffusion equation $ \partial_t u = \Delta^{1/2} (u^p)$ within a bounded area of space. For positive solutions that have smooth boundaries and satisfy the equation, we establish an optimal two-precise estimate for $u^q$ using the Sobolev inequality, where the values of $q$ and $p$ fall within a specific range between 0 and 2, inclusive. When $p$ equals 5, we determine the exact q value that results in an optimal two-precise estimate for $u^q$ and show that it is related to the exponent used in a different inequality related to the Sobolev inequality. We use this information to determine the rate at which the solutions from a related problem converge approach the average density of a two-fluid system.

Our VLA-COSMOS survey measured the polarization of 598 radio galaxies with a specific characteristics and we are presenting the data for 598 of those galaxies. The data shows a significant correlation between a property of the radio spectrum and the polarization of those galaxies. We are seeing a similar trend in other surveys, but our own survey shows a stronger relationship. Furthermore, we are seeing a stronger relationship between polarization and a property of the host galaxy's black hole in our own survey. Using mathematical models, we determined the distance at which polarization becomes more common and it corresponds to a specific scale out to a distance of 0.13 inches. Additionally, we calculated the average polarization of radio galaxies at different redshifts and we detected a break in this trend at a redshift of 1. The trend before this point follows our expected predictions. After adjusting some data to account for telescope limitations, we calculated the average polarization of radio galaxies at high redshifts and according to whether they are emitting flat or curved spectra. We saw polarization range of 0.1 to 1% in galaxies at very far distances. In our research, we selected radio galaxies that meet specific criteria to study the relationship between their luminosity and polarization. We discovered that radio galaxies' luminosity does not affect their polarization. Finally, using data from mid-infrared observations, we determined the relationship between radio galaxies' polarization and their luminosity and we detected a lack of highly polarized radio galaxies that also have high

We analyze the concept of uncertainty in information, quantified by entropy, and explore its mathematical underpinnings from an operational perspective relevant to security. To address this perspective, we consider a comprehensive system of probabilistic entropies that can be used to measure uncertainty and incorporate various security standards. The operations forming this system serve as a versatile tool to assess and compare entropy metrics, and facilitate tailored calculations of entropy under specific security constraints. Moreover, by categorizing security requirements, our framework, can tailor the operations within it to match particular security standards, and thereby, maximize entropy while adhering to those standards. The operations within our framework can also be used to compare and contrast different entropy metrics, and to calculate a comprehensive entropy metric that can accommodate multiple security standards.

The sub-grid energy transport in turbulent flows can be described by the difference between its local rate and a turbulent transport operator, which is based on the product of the auto-correlation of a velocity component and an advection term. Similar expressions apply to energy equations in both compressible and incompressible flows. By using this expression, the quasi-deterministic model derives a local heat flux model that is applicable to a wide range of turbulent flows. This model can also be applied to both sub-grid and semi-turbulent processes on a fine grid. In turbulent flows with energy spectra that follow a k^-5/3 form, the model-derived energy transport operator corresponds to the Kolmogorov-Mittag-Leffler transport operator. Furthermore, the model is found to accurately predict energy cascade rates in various types of turbulent flows, including natural convection, forced and anisotropic turbulence in square domains. Additionally, the model has also been applied to simulate semi-turbulent and sub-grid flows in compressible and incompressible contexts, with good agreement with numerical simulations and experimental data.

Conventional methods for fitting elastic scattering data are straightforward but have several limitations due to their simplicity; for example, they sometimes produce multiple solutions that fit the data equally well, such as in the $^{6}$Li case studied here. To address this issue, a novel approach is presented that incorporates statistical tools to determine the reliability of different fits and identify the most plausible one. As a practical application, this method is applied to the analyzed $^{6}$Li case to derive the most favored radial density of the $^{6}$Li ground state.

In a finite, non-asymptotic scenario, we investigate EM wave absorption by a perfectly resistive conductor in a 3D setting, finding its complex impedance and effective resistance. A thin slab of conductor was used to model the system, assuming geometric similarity and perfect electrical conductivity. By comparing thermal radiation from the slab to that of an ideal blackbody, we calculated its effective resistance and compare it to previous two-dimensional findings. Notably, we identify a need to refine traditional thermodynamic definitions to account for boundary effects. Additionally, we provide analysis on the influence of geometric constraints and non-asymptotic conditions on the emission and reflection spectra, deriving a novel approximation for high-frequency emissions that closely aligns with both theoretical and computational results. Furthermore, we compute the Q-factor of resonant spectra and propose a novel approximation. Alongside these theoretical findings, we discuss potential experimental applications and implications.

The rapid advancements in IoT and mobile devices have generated vast amounts of privately valued data, which necessitates precise privacy management to prevent sensitive information leakage. This work presents an innovative framework for quantifying privacy loss as a Bayesian network entropy change following FedSGD updates. The proposed framework addresses the limitations of previous research that failed to account for dependent data conditions in location-based services and mobile applications. It further demonstrates the computational and practical feasibility of the model using a representative dataset.

In recent years, a surge of research focused on using neural descriptors for place and topological navigation in LiDAR-based environments. This work presents an alternative, a neural descriptor transform specifically designed for 3D point clouds using integer arithmetic, allowing for both efficient and reliable place recognition and topological mapping in various places. Due to its compact format, the proposed descriptor can be either computed in hardware using edge devices or accessed directly from compressed neural data. This enables real-time place recognition and topological mapping without the need for additional processing, outperforming existing methods according to our evaluation on publicly available datasets. Moreover, the provided source code supports both application-independent and independent access to the proposed descriptor.

Advancements in neuroimaging technologies now enable detailed analysis of brain networks at an unprecedented resolution. Although this leads to richer statistical analysis possibilities, it also creates a need to adjust standard statistical methods to better suit these new datasets. In our research, we investigated how the inter-site effects present in functional connectivity affect the detection of individual and group differences. By examining data from the Human Connectome Project and altering standard connectivity-based classifiers under various conditions, we sought to gain a deeper understanding of the influence of inter-site effects on brain network analysis. Our findings suggest that while inter-site effects do impact the accuracy of connectivity-based classifiers, they are most reliably minimized when analyzing individual differences. Furthermore, we discovered that incorporating spatial information into the classification process successfully reduces the influence of inter-site effects and enhances the detection of individual and group differences. These outcomes offer valuable insights for optimizing the analysis of functional connectivity data and contribute to the development of data acquisition protocols with optimized sensitivity for the detection of individual and group differences.

In this paper, we present explicit, iterative algorithms solving the $\Lambda$-counting and -naming issues in the COMM model. These solutions work within a commutative monoid $(\oplus, \bot)$ where $\oplus$ represents a merge operation and $\bot$ denotes an absent value. The naming problem involves assigning unique values from a set to elements of a commutative monoid, whereas the counting problem involves determining the size of this set. Our algorithms are designed for a distributed environment consisting of $N$ stations with logarithmic energy consumption in each step ($O(\log N)$), resulting in an overall time complexity of $T \propto \sqrt{N} \log^2 N$ and energy consumption of $E \prolog N \cdot \log N$ for both problems.

This research presents a novel, multi-lingual language model called Mopass that utilizes positional encoding to overcome the limitations of current frame-based models, which do not account for positions during training. Additionally, our study investigates the effectiveness of using character-based units instead of word-based ones to address the problem of multi-lingual word mapping. Mopass achieves this by training a shared word-to-character mapping across languages and fine-tunes its cross-language word mapping using self-supervised, character-level objectives. In contrast to previous solutions, our model leverages positional encoding to capture positional context during training. Consequently, our framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art models on Google's CMU-MUST tool in 22 language pairs from 12 source languages.

We examine the isotope effect of H$_{3}$S using ab initio MD simulations, where we calculate the difference in its phase transition temperatures between H$_{3}^{70}$S and H$_{3}^{34}$S as a function of pressure, finding that the low-pressure contribution dominates at higher pressures but becomes negligible at extremely high pressures due to the low molar mass of the heavy isotopes. Consequently, the coefficient of the isotope effect ($\eta$) rises with pressure, primarily because of the increasing low molar mass contribution. Moreover, at any given pressure below 20 GPa, $\eta$ is substantially greater than its value at 20 GPa because of the high low molar mass contribution. Hence, $\eta$ is directly proportional to the molar mass of heavy isotopes and one should be cautious when using data from high-pressure scenarios to predict isotope effects at lower pressures due to their differing molar masses.

Obtaining an efficient motion plan in complex environments with numerous obstacles poses a significant challenge. We introduce an innovative strategy to create spatial constraints by utilizing learned probabilistic models, thereby reducing search space and outperforming existing methods in comparative evaluations. In this approach, a conditional variational autoencoder generates spatial constraints in the environment, enabling the system to utilize this information to create an octree search space and devise a localized motion plan. Our method outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of plan efficiency, query count, and success rate, especially in environments with high collision frequencies. Additionally, we demonstrate that our method can learn a data-driven policy for motion planning, resulting in faster and more efficient plans compared to other methods.

Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a crucial component with a long history in the field of computer vision. It has significant applications in fields like robotics and virtual environments. A promising method for improving overall performance is to enhance camera motion estimation through the use of learned scene descriptions. However, the focus of this approach has previously been limited to simple scenarios and it is not well understood how it performs in more complex and challenging situations. The challenges posed by the presence of objects like text or images protruding from a 3D scene are now being encountered more frequently, for example in the use of facade tagging for building design. The approach of using deep learning for learned descriptors has shown potential for large improvements, particularly in the challenging task of object-based 3D SLAM. The method outperformed other approaches in the simulation of a simple object-based scene and also showed its effectiveness in a realistic building simulation with textured objects. The data collected also revealed the impact of the method on the camera motion estimation, the quality of the learned descriptors, and the overall efficiency of the SLAM system. The results of this research contribute towards the development of an efficient and accurate object-based 3D SLAM system.

This research addresses the challenges associated with interference and limited transmit power in MIMO interference channels involving multiple users, through a optimization technique that involves a two-step process. First, the optimal solution for each user's precoder is determined by solving a LASSO-based optimization problem under group constraints. As a result, the approach not only enhances the sum-rate but also alleviates the curse of dimensionality by reducing the complexity and inter-user interference. Next, the optimal solution for each precoder is found by taking into account the DFT-based precoder structure, through a two-stage process of the blockwise LASSO and the Fast Fourier Transform. By iteratively applying these two methods, the approach achieves a significant decrease in power consumption and increases the sum-rate, outperforming approaches such as LASSO without group constraints and those that utilize DFT-based precoders without LASSO. Computational simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed technique in achieving improved performance and lower power consumption.

In this study, we investigate the impact of finite harmonic mappings ($\mathbb{C}$-linear transformations) on the pull-back of a rational function semiring, and its extension to a harmonic semiring, within the framework of tropical curves. Although the geometric results in this field are non-linear, the pull-back of certain semirings exhibits linear behavior. Non-degenerate linear transformations preserve the value of rational functions, and may alter the semi-ring of rational functions without preserving the value of rational functions. In contrast to continuous maps, harmonic mappings can alter the semi-ring of rational functions, and may not preserve the pull-back of rational functions. To address these cases of non-preserving pull-back, we establish that in all instances where the pull-back of rational functions is degenerate, it can be redefined additively over a lattice.

This research paper explores a specific class of measures within a Markov process, focusing on quasi-stationary distributions that maintain their relative stability in relation to the underlying killing measure. We establish precise conditions under which a unique quasi-stationary distribution exists, exhibiting exponential convergence in its transition dynamics. Building upon this foundation, a natural perturbation theorem is developed, enabling us to analyze small changes in parameters within Markov processes. This theoretical framework is applied to three distinct scenarios - killed Brownian motion, killed L\'evy processes, and birth-and-death processes.

Building upon the findings of Arunadati Saigal, a method is formulated to compute a specific type of invariant for knots, incorporating certain elements of the knot invariant realm that are similar to the Tutte polynomial but tied to the Reeb space, a component of the knot's structural analysis. Notably, this new approach can provide information about the Reeb space's topological characteristics when certain conditions are met. A comparison is drawn with the established form of the knot's invariant, revealing a connection to the twisted Alexander polynomials and the Resistance Conjecture. Additionally, two distinct mathematical integrals are derived, one tied to the variation of a specific mathematical object and another tied to the volume of a specific region, both originating from the Reeb space. One of these integrals is found to align with the findings of a different topological analysis, Heegaard-Floater's, while further research is needed to understand the significance of the other integral, believed to be tied to the properties of a specific surface, a pseudo-Anosov projective torus knot invariant.

We've utilized a novel elastoresistance technique to monitor the sound velocities within iron-based superconductors, particularly in non-superconducting metals like NaFeAs and LiFeAs. Our research reveals that the speed of sound waves in LiFeAs has similar properties to NaFeAs near its transition, indicating a more established nematic phase in LiFeAs. Additionally, we've detected an unconventional elastoresistance pattern in NaFeAs showing temperature independence, suggesting it's linked to nematic fluctuations rather than structural deformity. These findings imply NaFeAs and LiFeAs exhibit distinct nematic states, supporting the association between correlated electronic activity and symmetry-breaking nematic order.

This study evaluates a range of one-loop numerical corrections for Higgs and Z boson production in association with a top quark within Type-II two Higgs doublet models. The calculations take into account a full 2HDM scenario, meeting theoretical requirements and incorporating one-loop corrections for critical elements, such as top quark and gluon dynamics, as well as lightest physical Higgs and charged scalar behaviors. The results show that while corrections may be sizable for certain parameter spaces meeting sensitivity and planar constraints, most remain within experimental uncertainty for most 2HDM scenarios. However, for a broad set of parameters not meeting these constraints, one-loop corrections often become prominent, especially for moderate to large gluon-fusion contributions. Furthermore, in a scenario meeting all constraints, even though loop-level corrections are minimal for on-shell production of the lightest physical Higgs and top quark through gluon-fusion, this doesn't extend to the dominant channel of quark-antiquark fusion leading to similar states. Consequently, in the total production cross-section of Higgs or top quarks via both gluon-fusion and quark-antiquark fusion, loop-level corrections often become prominent even when the input Higgs or top quark is on-shell.

Building complex 3D structures from basic materials requires creativity, but artificial intelligence can facilitate innovative design by automating the decision-making process. Artificial muscles provide an ideal platform to create these complex structures, but their geometry makes optimization challenging. To tackle this problem, a novel application of deep reinforcement learning is proposed to learn optimal assembly strategies for 3D structures. By analyzing both directed and exploratory design approaches, the AI model can develop creative solutions for new and existing structure designs. Key innovations include the use of a specific algorithmic technique and a novel learning environment that simulates the creative process. This method not only enhances our understanding of artificial intelligence in design, but also reveals new insights into material assembly and geometric manipulation. Ultimately, these innovations open doors to novel applications in architecture, medicine, and other fields.

Flavor-symmetric confining vacua in chiral gauge theories must satisfy a set of critical equations - the Vafa-Witten 't Hooft anomaly matching equations. By utilizing the representation theory of the gauge group and its phase relationships, we establish a systematic framework for solving these equations in general, non-Abelian cases. This analytical framework provides a comprehensive understanding of the center symmetry transformations and its implications for charge operators. Applying this framework to theories with $SU(N)$ gauge groups, we derive new explicit conditions on the superpotential for various representations, representing significant advancements over previous studies. Furthermore, our results are found to complement an existing study on the representation theory of the gauge group and flavor symmetry by Bhubaneswar Theiga Pati.

We establish the Navier-Stokes equations' well-posedness in certain critical Besov spaces and periodic Besov spaces. Specifically, we demonstrate that the equations remain well-posed under specific conditions in spaces such as $\dot{B}_{2, 2}^{-2}$ and $\dot{P}\dot{B}_{2, 2}^{0}$. Additionally, we show that the solution to the equations belongs to a specific space called $C(0, L^{2})$. Our results are then extended to a more complex system of equations known as the Navier-Stokes equations with zero-tracer conditions on the surface of the 3D ball. We also use our findings to derive the well-posedness of the Boussinesq system. A key aspect of our work is the use of a new approach for deriving the well-posedness of the equations, which involves a combination of the simple-stokes method and the use of the $ext{P}$ projector. Our work significantly expands on the existing results by proving the well-posedness of the equations in a wider range of spaces than what has been achieved previously.

A detailed investigation of the thermal response in the antiferromagnetic phase of the dilute quantum Heisenberg magnet Ce$_{0.45}$Yb$_{0.55}$Al$_3$. The research, conducted using inelastic neutron scattering over a wide temperature range, reveals that temperature-dependent magnon bandgap and resonance modes within the system undergo a significant change due to thermal magnon interaction. These observations are well-supported by simulations based on the spin-wave model and additional theoretical calculations involving the thermal broadening of the magnon spectrum according to the spin-momentum locking principle. The study also provides direct visualisation of the meron mode at low energy and confirms its existence alongside the high-energy resonance mode previously identified within Ce$_{0.45}$Yb$_{0.55}$Al$_3$. The study provides new insights into the antiferromagnetic phase associated with the Heisenberg-like spin model in this system.

This research proposes an optimized Guedira GQ GQ- variant GQ+ cryptosystem by incorporating an extended Galois field with a prime p greater than 2. The system incorporates q = p^2 as the size of the public-key and a modified polynomial f(x) = x^2 + x + 1 with a degree of n = p. The study utilizes the computational efficiency of the multithreaded capability of Java to enhance security, reducing potential attacks from the increase in the value of p. In this context, the research introduces an algorithm for generating random numbers within the field $\mathbb{F}_p$, applies linear change of variables to the modified elliptic curve defined by the quartic polynomial $g(y) = (x+1)^4 + (y+1)^4 - 2(x+y)$ with A=1, B=1, C=0, D=0, E=0, F=0, G=0 at point (0,0) in $\mathbb{F}_p^2$, and develops a method for efficiently computing the inverse of elements in the field $\mathbb{F}_p$. The modifications result in increased public-key size, information transmission rates, and computational complexity but offer enhanced security through larger prime numbers. The research refines security by employing a random number-based change of variables at the decryption stage, making it computationally infeasible for adversaries to achieve a useful time-based attack frequency

Language models often struggle with uncommon words (words appearing less than 5 times per million in the training data) because they're rarely encountered during training. Although neural language models gain some understanding of these words through context, this process is limited by their reliance on word2vec representations, which don't fully capture rare word semantics. As a result, there's a lack of consensus about how to effectively handle these words. This research aims to clear up some common misunderstandings in rare word handling by demonstrating that "no special handling needed" is actually a valid approach. To support this claim, we develop an unsupervised method for large vocabulary learning that leverages sentence-level meaning to improve rare word embeddings beyond what word2vec can achieve. Our proposed LVK method combines word and sentence-based models to effectively learn large vocabulary words. Furthermore, by combining our learned word embeddings with contextualized representations, we show that it's possible to surpass GPT-2's performance on understanding rare words through context, thus enhancing natural language generation with more accurate and less artificial results.

For a weighted directed graph with unit edge weights, a random Minimum Spanning Acycle is examined. This cycle-like structure is an extension of the more familiar Minimum Spanning Tree found in undirected graphs. This researcher explores the statistical behavior of the extremal weights within the MSAC and demonstrates that they converge towards a specific Gaussian distribution when properly scaled. Additionally, it is noted that this result is analogous to a corresponding finding by Erdős and Szemerédi on extremal weights in Minimum Spanning Trees.

This study presents a comprehensive privacy vulnerability against vertical FL protocols, impacting users in both server-client and federated multi-agent settings. We showcase robust inference-based attacks using generated synthetic data, revealing that with access to a single user's partial data and overall distribution, attackers can make nearly perfect predictions for the remaining data components. Experiments conducted across three applications highlight that these attacks significantly exceed the FL model's learning capacity in multiple scenarios. To mitigate this vulnerability, we propose an enhanced vertical FL protocol incorporating data discretization, thereby substantially enhancing user privacy security while achieving up to a 10% loss in FL performance.

Utilizing the light-cone quark-diquark-antiquark description and the Bethe-Salpeter equation, researchers derived a precise formula for the $B^+ \to p \bar{\Lambda}(1555)$ transition form factor across a broad range of momentum transfers using the instanton-induced chiral quark formalism and the dressing function from the Wendel-Soto model. Subsequently, these findings were applied to calculate the decay width of the $B^+ \to p \bar{\Lambda}(1555)$ process in two distinct scenarios: one in which the dressings are incorporated directly, and another in which the mass and effective coupling of the dark antibaryon, $\bar{q}qq$, are treated as free parameters with their relationship governed by a sum rule. Notably, our work yielded decay widths of approximately 2.95 (6.69) $10^{-10}$ GeV for $\bar{q}q$ ($\bar{s}s$) dark antibaryons with a mass of 1.55 (1.70) GeV and an effective coupling of 2.33 (4.20). By comparing this with recent experimental form factor data obtained from the BESIII collaboration for the $B^+ \to p \bar{\Lambda}$ transition, researchers identified a possible candidate for the dark antibaryon with mass 1.55 GeV and effective coupling 2.33 as the most suitable among

Research on defending a network of urban areas against massive attacks has historically been focused on a single modus operandum for the adversary, limiting the effectiveness of defensive strategies. This oversight is further exacerbated when agencies responsible for defense allocate resources differently, impairing the overall response. Our study introduces a comprehensive agent-based model (ABM) to simulate urban defense and countermeasure implementation. Unlike previous research, our city model incorporates multiple adversary tactics and allows various government agencies to dynamically redistribute resources in pursuit of optimal outcomes. This multi-agent, multi-armored-vehicle reward-based algorithm empowers agencies to allocate resources efficiently and effectively combat multiple types of attacks. Our results, obtained via simulation, validate the importance of a adaptive resource allocation in ensuring urban safety.

This study examines the theoretical connections between gravity, electromagnetism and entanglement, applying the concept of entanglement to a specific black hole scenario situated within a spherical cavity. We explore how the electric potential of the boundary influences the first order phase transition characteristics of the black hole. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of the magnetic field arising from the magnetic type scalar field on this transition phenomenon.

This research introduces a novel bag sampling approach to speed up Michelson hashing for indexing lengthy documents, substantially enhancing long document ranking results while maintaining efficiency in retrieving short documents. A comparative analysis with traditional Michelson hashing was conducted using the Google Code Search index, demonstrating that our method achieves equivalent query times despite requiring slightly longer construction times. Consequently, this technique is ideally suited for search applications on distant devices with limited resources.

Currently, there is a lack of semi-supervised node classification methods for Graph Neural Networks that can effectively handle edge-weighted graphs. Many existing methods, including a widely cited approach based on the pseudo-labeling technique, suffer from shortcomings. This research reveals that the pseudo-labeling method struggles to achieve good results due to label noise caused by biased estimation. This study introduces an Edge-weighted Graph Neural Network that addresses these issues by propagating labels based on a degree-weighted averaging technique. Experimental results using seven benchmark edge-weighted datasets demonstrate that E-GNN is the top performer when compared to existing semi-supervised node classification methods. The associated code has been made available for public access.

The use of betatron radiation as an X-ray source is highly advantageous due to its precise control over plasma focus devices, despite previously overlooked beam dynamics that affect performance. We investigate the influence of plasma center mismatch and off-axis acceleration in twisted fields on radiation quality, finding that an optimal twist can enhance X-ray photon flux and critical energy by significant factors. These improvements also result in increased coherent X-ray photon flux of $1.31\times 10^{8}$ photons per second, an enhanced critical energy of $2.38$ keV, and an increased photon flux of $1.43\times 10^{11}$ photons per second across the entire energy spectrum at 10 MeV.

This paper introduces a new method for privately learning deep trees, overcoming previous limitations where accuracy levels often fluctuated or declined with growing dataset sizes. A revised approach, preserving node diversity, is presented and analyzed. Empirical evidence shows the proposed method outperforms its predecessor in terms of prediction accuracy, achieving up to a 40% higher accuracy rate while maintaining a comparable level of privacy. Furthermore, the revised method's accuracy improves as the dataset grows, exceeding the previous method's results by 25% with large datasets.

We introduce a revised moment-matching algorithm for optimizing a regularized R\'enyi divergence, allowing for the analysis of singular values within the primal-dual objective under low-rank constraints, enabling the revision of existing worst-case convergence rates for generators, optimizers, and R\'enyi divergences. By building upon the Primal-Dual Splitting algorithm, our algorithm rigorously maintains the parametric form of solutions from the original problem. It is then demonstrated that our algorithm achieves improved convergence for both Euclidean and R\'enyi divergences, with rates potentially exceeding those of the Optimal Transport metric. Furthermore, our algorithm has been successfully applied to solve a real-world problem in compressive sensing.

Chaiat and Vandekar (2020) introduced product Dirichlet priors for model and parameter estimation in model selection for dependent categorical data. We build upon this work by applying product Dirichlet priors to dependent categorical data with an unspecified space. Our method estimates models and parameters for dependent categorical data without specifying a model for its spatial structure. We demonstrate its efficacy by performing an analysis of a childhood leukemia study to determine if and to what degree the environment influences the incidence of leukemia. Our results show that the estimated models and prior weights accurately capture the underlying associations in the data.

Researchers have re-examined the heavy ball method, a proven algorithm for minimizing smooth, strongly convex functions. By incorporating a damping coefficient, they have developed an approach capable of achieving superior convergence rates under specific Yudin-Vieta conditions for convex functions. A key aspect of this method involves choosing the damping coefficient carefully, as an improperly selected value can result in a slower convergence rate than expected. Interestingly, the algorithm exhibits an optimal convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}^+ \left( \exp \left( - \frac{c}{\Delta^2} \cdot K_n^2 n \right) \right)$, where $c$ is a constant related to the function's properties, $\Delta$ is the smoothness constant, $K_n$ is the $n$-th Kronecker coefficient, and $n$ is the dimensionality of the space. This rate is superior to what is achieved by the standard gradient descent method. A practical application of this method can be seen in the minimization of quadratic functions, where the addition of damping can facilitate entry-wise monotonicity, useful in fields like clustering and feature selection.

This study investigates the general algorithms for a visually guided robot that follows a wall. A realistic simulation environment is used to evaluate various algorithms while considering two critical factors: the sensor's capabilities and limitations. The finite field of view of a distance sensor is taken into account, which a moving robot may encounter, resulting in a distorted trajectory when using algorithms that adjust speed based on distance. Moreover, this study assesses the increased complexity of the back-end control system caused by sensor limitations. To overcome these issues, this research proposes two simple solutions: the'reduce turn angle' method and the 'path reconstruction' method. The latter method offers a more straightforward implementation and greater robustness, but requires more computational power. Experimental results indicate that these proposed algorithms enable a robot to achieve successful wall-following regardless of sensor capabilities, resulting in a more consistent and precise trajectory.

In a superconducting bag model of doped cuprates, where microwaves induce a non-equilibrium gap state that blocks their penetration, below a critical frequency cones of quasiparticles open up to a larger volume of momentum space than above this frequency, creating non-equilibrium scenarios regardless of doping level despite the same gap parameter being used across all cases. This model simplifies understanding of terahertz spectroscopy and quantum oscillations in heavy fermion superconductors and can also explain penetration depth anomalies in cuprates and other superconductors, with its estimates closely matching experimental values, notably the penetration depth of YNi2B4S4 which this model places at around 20 nanometers.

This paper examines the two-level finite element approach for a family of curvature flows under non-reflection conditions across convex interfaces, and establishes the optimal error estimates for both space and time, which confirms a previously unproved theorem by Zhou et al. in \cite{ZLLQ20}.

Recent breakthroughs in robotics and automation often rely on learning algorithms,
while biology and pharmacology increasingly utilize experimental techniques.
This research paper employs a novel combination of these two fields by
developing a control system for plant movement and growth based on
reinforcement learning.
Using a virtual environment built from data collected through MRI and 3D
reconstructions, the system aims to achieve specific objectives, such as maximizing
a plant's head position or opening its pinnae as much as possible.
Successful results from simulated and real-world tests validate the proposed
approach and showcase its potential in biology and pharmacology applications.

The large-scale properties of simple three-dimensional shapes, randomly generated with certain constraints, are studied. Specifically, we analyze the large-scale properties of two types of these shapes: those that incorporate simple three-dimensional shapes, and those that do not. In both cases, we find that the large-scale properties can be described by a unique set of statistical mechanics-like equations. Our findings also suggest that the large-scale properties of these shapes coincide with the predicted properties of a fundamental physical system, the so-called Euclidean Hydrodynamic Triangle Network. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the large-scale properties of randomly embedded three-dimensional loops, in the large N limit, give rise to the same large-scale properties as those of the simplest type of these shapes, thus implying that their behavior is dominated by the underlying mesh.

High-throughput quantitative image analysis holds significant potential for significant improvements in accurate diagnoses and treatments in oncology, but it is hindered by inconsistencies in quantification methods. To fully utilize the shroud of imaging information, in-depth analysis of tumor characteristics is essential, yet subjecting large datasets to visual inspection is impractical and impairs diagnostic precision. Radiomics has emerged as a promising approach, but its application is hampered by discrepancies resulting from varying quantification techniques. To overcome these challenges, the development of standardized, automated, and reliable algorithms is crucial for image quantification. In this study, we employed a state-of-the-art, deep learning approach, specifically deep regression, to design a and robust image quantification system, thereby eliminating the need for manual input or correction. We evaluated the performance of our method on two distinct breast cancer datasets, with a focus on quantitative feature extraction, and we report our results.

Our calculations using the kaon-baryon coupled-channel approach and the isobar model have analyzed the $\gamma p \to K^+\Sigma^0$ reaction cross section across the second and third resonance peaks. The latter was primarily attributed to the $Y_2175(1/2-)$ and $Y_2175(3/2-)$ $\Sigma^0$-containing amplitudes. Inclusion of $K^+\Sigma^-$ in the calculation also led to notable contributions, mainly from the $Y_2175(1/2-)$ with the right couplings. This is consistent with the observed energy dependence of the $\gamma p \to K^+ \Sigma^0$ differential cross section. In contrast, the second peak was mainly due to the single $\Sigma^0$ resonance, namely the $Y_2175(1/2-)$, with no significance from $K^+$-$\Sigma^-$ interference. This is also reflected in the shape of the $K^+\Sigma^0 \pi^0$ differential cross section. Additionally, the predicted branching ratio of $Y_2175(1/2-)$ decaying to $K^+\Sigma^0$ is about 6%, much lower than what has been observed experimentally. A thorough discussion on this discrepancy is provided.

The success of downstream applications within NLP relies heavily on the quality of data preprocessing. Like any other component in an NLP pipeline, a pre-processing tool can also experience improvements over time. Consequently, there is a need to develop a method for evaluating its effectiveness and to pinpoint areas that necessitate enhancement or correction. In this paper, we outline a general approach for assessing and refining pre-processing tools, illustrated by our experience with correcting the English BERT segmentation pre-processing tool supplied by Spark NLP. Our investigation encompassed over 47,000 words discovered through 228,000 Google search queries, involving 414 distinct words, spanning 1,260 distinct word forms, and employing 1,510 distinct separators. The findings indicate that the original segmentation algorithm made a total of 3,835 errors. In addition to describing the tools used in this research, we outline a step-by-step guide for replicating these results and freely provide the employed pre-processing tool along with the BERT models used in this study via publicly accessible GitHub repositories.

We re-examine a theory that aims to combine aspects of dark energy and dark matter, incorporating a modified version of the $R^2$ gravity theory. A new feature in this revised framework involves coupling modified gravity to a complex scalar field with variable mass. By analyzing the stability of cosmological fluctuations within the framework, we discover a fundamental fluctuation mode that shares similarities with a particle of approximately 414 grams. Our findings indicate that this revised theory has the potential to explain both dark energy and dark matter, suggesting that the universe could be in a de-Sitter phase due to a fundamental scalar field with a negative kinetic energy density. Furthermore, when the cross-over temperature is around 4400K, the revised theory can account for both phenomena through the generation of matter.

We suggest using a Gaussian latent variable model to understand student enrollment patterns in a computational way. This type of model generates data by combining course means and student abilities, which are linked to course attributes and student demographics, respectively. This framework generalizes existing models and we developed an algorithm based on variational data augmentation to estimate model parameters. This algorithm incorporates stochastic gradient ascent and expectation-maximization methods. We applied our model to examine enrollment trends at Stanford between 1994 and 2009, uncovering significant course mean shifts and major demographic changes. In particular, by modeling Stanford's course offerings from 1994 to 2009, our approach revealed detailed patterns of course mean shifts. Moreover, our model accurately predicted student ability based on student demographics and estimated the uncertainty associated with student ability matrices. These findings highlight the value of our approach in understanding Stanford's course offerings over time and in generating predictive distributions for future enrollment patterns based on demographic profiles.

This study investigates the outcome of a zero-sum game with two players participating in vehicle platooning. To achieve a stable equilibrium, Pontryagin's principle is utilized to determine the best course of action for each player. By defining the leader as the first vehicle and the follower as the second, with the leader seeking to minimize time delay and the follower seeking to minimize spatial error between vehicles, the study derives the optimal values for these variables. The outcomes show that when the leader-follower spacing is optimal, the time delays for both players are equivalent, which aligns with previous research. Furthermore, when one player cannot deviate from their actions without increasing their costs, the other player achieves the best outcome by mimicking the leader's actions, resulting in optimal vehicle spacing occurring at the same level as the leader-follower spacing. The study's findings are validated through numerical analysis and visual representation.

In order to gain a deeper understanding of convex SGD algorithms when applied to smooth objectives, researchers have been exploring a general purpose, model-free method for analyzing its local convergence behavior. This new approach, called the variational formalism, has made it possible for researchers to reformulate the effects of SGD on the behavior of its variations. This paper presents an enhancement to this method, called CA-SGD, which can alter the convergence characteristics of SGD to reach a more accurate solution. The enhancement is specifically tested on a logistic regression problem and the results show that CA-SGD is capable of achieving improved solutions, both in terms of accuracy and convergence, when applied to binary logistic regression with a large number of categories.

This study compares the ability of various transformer models to detect whether news headlines were written by humans or generated by machines. Eight models, driven by enthusiasm from recent advancements in transformer technology, were tested. The examination utilized datasets comprising both multilingual and single-language news articles. The analysis revealed that the largest models performed exceptionally well, demonstrating high accuracy across languages. The results showed that human-written headlines can be distinguished from computer-generated ones with 95% or higher certainty. The analysis also revealed that certain characteristics, such as length and punctuation usage, can help set human-written headlines apart from machine-generated ones. Based on the findings, the GPT2-ru model proved to be the most effective at identifying human-written headlines, achieving a success rate of 96.6%, and is therefore recommended for use in automated news verification systems.

We employ a straightforward graphical method to evaluate the density of an odd number of plaquettes in a specific lattice pattern and find it leads to the formation of gaps within chiral spin liquids. Our method also indicates that in an equilateral triangle grid, the density of these odd plaquettes is always at a minimum. This has a practical implication that in patterns generated from the triangle pattern through rotations of 60 degrees, the density of these odd plaquettes is always at its highest. This leads to the discovery that the odd and even gaps within certain materials close to the point where the density reaches its highest are related to a different ordering than the one that occurs at the density of its lowest. This outcome contradicts previous predictions that the two ordering types are equivalent. This new method can be used to determine the type of ordering that occurs within certain materials by calculating the density of these odd plaquettes and comparing it to what is expected in an ideal, uniform situation. This new method is particularly useful for understanding the properties of certain materials that exhibit a unique type of gap within their structure, and it may also be used to understand other types of gap within other materials that exhibit a similar type of behavior.

A key advantage of redundant arrays with N antennas, including the SKA, lies in its ability to mitigate systematic effects and realize real-time calibration schemes - leading to significantly reduced antenna gain variances in real-time contexts. We investigate how this same redundancy impacts the correlations between antenna gains and examine how it influences the total gain variance in arrays with various configurations, characterized by their angular distances between antennas. We find that for narrow spacings, the gain variances actually increase with the number of antennas, before decreasing significantly in more widely spaced arrays. We further show how these findings impact the noise floor of the SKA and discuss the implications for the SKA's real-time calibration capabilities.

Machine learning methods, particularly deep neural networks, can be utilized to resolve portfolio allocation issues. In this context, an autoencoding generative adversarial network (ACGAN) was devised to enhance the Markowitz model by incorporating an additional feature - future returns. To do this, the ACGAN was combined with a Markowitz-based optimization technique and evaluated using S\&P 500 stocks over four time periods. Compared to the traditional Markowitz method, the ACGAN yielded enhanced portfolio outcomes, quantifiable in returns increases of 0.3%, 0.5%, 0.7%, and 0.9% respectively. Consequently, the ACGAN proved effective in augmenting the Markowitz framework and revealing the ACGAN's potential as a decision-making tool.

The QCD transition from $n_{f}=3$ to $n_{f}=4$ in the center-of-mass energy range
of about $2.4$ to $6.3$ GeV in the Variable Flavour Number Scheme (VFNS) is
investigated using the scenario of three active flavours with massless quarks,
except for the bottom quark with a mass of $4$ GeV. Employing renormalization group
equations with three and four active flavours and considering both the renormalization
group invariant energy scale and $\overline{\mbox{MS}}$ scheme with a common scale
$\mu$, these observables are computed accurately. A comparison is performed of how
the phase transition can be felt at Future Electron-Proton Colliders in comparison to
the FCC-hh and LHC. A discussion also includes the quantum jump of decoupling at
the onset of the QCD transition in the FPP in contrast to the FCC-hh and LHC. A
prediction also made of $\Delta \mbox{Q}_{\mbox{S}}^{\mbox{ij}}(N)$ in the QCD
transition at the three active flavours with a massless quark, except for the bottom
quark with a mass of $4$ GeV, in the $\overline{\mbox{MS}}$ scheme at the onset
of the QCD transition at the FCC

High-capacity neural networks with Bayesian methods offer an attractive alternative to traditional approaches for handling sparse and class-dominated data sets in classification tasks. Theoretical research suggests that using a Bayesian neural network with categorical labels and categorical priors will converge towards a Bayes risk minimum, albeit with categorical labels leading to Bayesian neural network predictions that are themselves categorical. This categorization may cause the network to overlook continuous cues beneficial for learning, suggesting the need for techniques producing more continuous outputs from neural networks. Categorical labels on regression tasks have been addressed in prior research, but this study classifies data and therefore necessitates the development of a method catering to this specific application. The introduced approach uses an intermediate layer to produce a probability distribution over classes for a specific data point, effectively providing a distribution 'weight' to classify samples. This technique maintains the benefits of Bayesian neural network inference, yielding accurate and well-justified predictions on a balanced data set and improving upon prior methods in classification tasks. Notably, this approach also accommodates estimation uncertainty in classification decisions, making it easier to integrate with existing belt-level beliefs and providing a discrete alternative to the batch posterior sampling algorithm. The provided implementation includes variational sampling methods for categorical belief estimation, catered to neural networks with categorical labels and spherical output layers. A detailed rationale and guidance on implementation have been provided in the appendix for readers. Despite numerous automated tools available to extract and translate social media content across different languages, a significant barrier still exists for users to access content protected by access restrictions. This content, often restricted by CAPTCHAs, requires users to prove their intentions to access it. This study aims to innovate machine translation systems by developing a method that combines translation and CAPTCHA-breaking techniques in tandem, allowing an English sentence to be translated into another language while simultaneously bypassing the CAPTCHA to access the target content. This novel approach is dubbed 'Torch,' stands for Translation to Open Content, and is a two-stage system that utilizes a pre-existing machine translator and a CAPTCHA-busting model. In a comprehensive evaluation, Torch demonstrated exceptional performance, translating English sentences over multiple languages while successfully bypassing CAPTCHAs in over 90% of cases, making it a cutting-edge solution for users to access diverse multilingual social media content.

In various fields, weighted networks have been used to model intricate relationships. This survey focuses on weighted hypergraphs, which are generalizations of multi-component graphs, to derive a comprehensive framework that enables the calculation of spectral characteristics. Two key approaches - extending algebraic operators and generalizing stochastic matrices - have been developed to study random walks and transience in weighted hypergraphs. Additionally, we built upon the tensor join to expand the spectral decomposition of weighted hypergraphs, allowing the representation of highly degenerate eigenvalue problems. This was then applied to derived algorithms for computing the second eigenvalue and eigenvectors, as well as the Laplacian spectrum, in weighted hypergraphs. Finally, we employed numerical examples to illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

INSIST, a space telescope, is in orbit around the Sun alongside Gaia. Its circular field of view is about 11 degrees in diameter, and it observes Gaia's secondary sky measurements. INSIST's main aim is to discover thousands of distant transfer stars that will be used to determine Gaia's lateral displacement during the mission. These transfer stars are initially identified on ground-based images. However, these images lack the quality needed to confirm the presence of these stars unambiguously. This paper discusses the method used to improve image quality through a combination of spreading out the light from these stars and enhancing image clarity using algorithms. The algorithm's test resulted in an effective increase in image quality of about two times the limit at which these stars can be confidently identified on average, averaging at 19.4 magnitude. This is comparable to the quality of Hubble Space Telescope's images. INSIST's fully functional image combines Gaia's N=5 measurements, three of which are taken in parallel to the Sun's center, and its operational phase is expected to last about six months from Gaia's May 2018 launch.

In clinical trials, continuous outcomes often exhibit temporal patterns,
which are frequently addressed by modeling observations as a combination of
baseline values, time-related factors, and error terms. While the use of
natural cubic splines in longitudinal data analysis can capture complex
relationships, it is common for only a subset of available time points to be
measured, resulting in significant estimation inefficiency and substantial bias
when employing restricted maximum likelihood estimation or residual maximum likelihood
estimation within an unbiased optional stopping principle framework.
Constrained maximum likelihood estimation, which incorporates constraints on the
optional stopping trajectory, can mitigate these issues, yielding more precise
estimates. This paper utilizes simulated data in both continuous and dichotomous
forms to compare constrained and unrestricted methods, highlighting the
substantial estimation efficiency improvements and decreased bias that arise from
its use. Further, constrained maximum likelihood estimation is implemented within
both R and SAS platforms.

A novel technique called conformational space annealing has been developed to enhance the thoroughness of reaction pathway calculations. This method, which involves increasing the width of the energy grid during simulations, enables more efficient sampling of reaction pathways. As a supplementary tool, an updated version of the PATHAIR program has been released, incorporating both CSSA and a revised version of the path-finding algorithm, to provide more accurate and efficient calculations. The updated program is available for download on the BDCAT website.

In this research, we establish sharp $L^{n/(n-1)}$ estimates for a specified parabolic Hessian equation, tying the outcome to the entire, non-negative subsolution theory of the related elliptic equation. Specifically for quadratic forms, we devise a boundary control method to derive these estimates, providing a new approach since traditional methods within elliptic regularity are ineffective due to the absence of symmetric diffusion. Additionally, our findings yield sharp maximum principles for both the parabolic equation and its dual.

A well-established link exists between the expressions of simply typed lambda-calculus and boolean algebra, except for one type - the unit type. This gap is bridged using a language construct called Church encodings. This relationship raises questions regarding how certain properties inherent to lambda-calculus affect boolean algebra and vice versa. This paper focuses on one of these queries: do certain properties of boolean algebra, when translated to lambda-calculus, result in corresponding properties for simply typed lambda-calculus? We investigate this by examining a range of boolean algebra properties that can be represented through Church encodings and, in doing so, refrains from addressing the converse question.

This study applies the Lions-type measure derivative to two types of nonlinear equations: one involving the Lévy area and another being a stochastic differential equation. Our work explores conditions for these equations to have unique solutions and possess a maximum absolute value, which is capped at a given limit. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the integrals of their respective measures of variation. Notably, the variation measure of the Lévy area is shown to exceed that of the Stratonovich integral, including in the isometry context.

This research explores topological properties of $H(K)$-groups, where $H(K)$ denotes the set of normal subgroups $N$ in a group $G$ such that for every finite set $S$ within $G$, the intersection of $N$ and the normalizer of $S$ in $G$ is limited to $K$. Specifically, the study introduces $H(K)$-groups and examines their hull-kernel-type topology, particularly focusing on the lower separation axioms and compactness. In this context, the investigation also relates $H(K)$-groups to quasi-Baumslag groups and generalized Baer groups. Additionally, the research involves finding essential theorems regarding the open sets in $H(K)$-groups, as well as distinct topological characteristics of certain subgroups, including Lagrange subgroups, divisible groups, nilpotent groups, and abelian groups. Finally, the study specifically handles Baer groups and establishes distinct topological properties for them.

The development of a database requires significant investment in ensuring its robustness. However, no research has been conducted to explore executive abilities outside of the original context in which the database was created. This study addresses this gap by developing a framework to support executive abilities, particularly where databases lack essential data. Based on two large datasets from YFSearch and TREC Data-to-Document, our method demonstrates higher accuracy compared to current best practices, specifically by ascertaining that including more ingredients in a dish doesn't always enhance its taste and safely removing a laptop's hard drive doesn't affect its internal data storage capabilities. To achieve this progress, a novel approach is taken where natural language descriptions of concepts, like frisbee's impact on grass, work in tandem with precise definitions through trusty references like Wikipedia to form solid, informative queries that are subsequently processed using a powerful encoder, like BERT to produce refined, authoritative subsampling candidates that are eventually ranked using a clever scores aggregation technique. This methodology facilitates systems to intelligently draw upon external knowledge to fill in the gaps within a dataset, effectively utilizing supplementary information from sources, like Wikipedia, to enhance a system's overall understanding and fill in the missing pieces of a system. As an added benefit, this methodology also opens up the door for developing systems to efficiently draw upon large, public sources, like Wikipedia, to fill in the missing pieces of a system and fill in the missing pieces of a system.
