In a hybrid quantum system using a quantum dot array and a bosonic cQED system, 
the Fermi-Hubbard model can be simulated on a superconducting anode array. 
The model describes interacting fermions in a lattice structure. 
The experiment involves mapping fermions into bosonic harmonics in a quantum cavity, 
which interacts equally with each dot in the array via a two-photon transition. 
The CQED system acts as a mediator in the simulation by enabling interactions 
between fermions and a higher fermionic level. 
The exchange of photons between dots allows for the mapping of fermionic hopping 
on the dot lattice, effectively simulating fermionic hopping in a lattice structure. 
The approach enables a controlled quantum simulation of the Fermi-Hubbard model 
that compromises neither system's capabilities nor the capabilities to measure qubits. 
The quantum simulation process involves a sequence of operations that leverage the strengths 
of both the quantum dot array and the CQED system, resulting in an exchange interaction 
between a single fermion and multiple fermions, as well as fermionic hopping. 
The latter process, though observed through a single qubit measurement, 
exhibits distinct characteristics from its analog counterpart, offering a new path 
for understanding complex quantum phenomena in a controllable and replicable setting.

This study introduces a generalized definition of the matching polynomial for complete graphs and complete bipartite graphs, extending the established notions for complete graphs. We examine properties of the generalized matching polynomial for complete graphs and bipartite graphs, as well as its associated Laplace polynomials and Hessian determinants. Additionally, we provide Demetrovian characterization formulas for complete graphs, incomplete bipartite graphs, and certain subgraphs of complete bipartite graphs, in terms of their generalized matching polynomials and Laplace polynomials.

Building on Axler and Pearson's research, we investigate representations of the finite index subgroups of the mapping class group that are associated with pseudo-Anosov elements, and demonstrate that these representations fall into two broad categories. We further show that the symmetric invariant space within the unit circle closure of each such representation is finite-dimensional.

This study examines the impact of adopted Scrum methodologies on the success of software projects conducted fully remotely, comparing them to traditional in-office projects. Our research indicates that remote Scrum projects are less likely to achieve success than their in-office counterparts, with a notable failure rate disparity. Furthermore, we found that remote Scrum projects tend to struggle compared to both remote and in-office projects that employ Scrum. Our analysis suggests that these outcomes can be attributed to remote Scrum projects' increased difficulty in maintaining communication and control, resulting from the lack of face-to-face interaction and frequent meetings. These challenges are magnified by the inability to easily switch between work and meeting modes. These findings offer valuable insights for teams considering Scrum implementation in a remote setting.

This research delves into the properties of arrowhead matrices, with a focus on their eigenvectors. We explore specific eigenvalues arising from these matrices and express certain eigenvectors in terms of parameter-dependent equations. Additionally, we establish connections to Gau--Wu numbers, Gau--Wu matrices, and related theories.

Measurements of long-distance quantum fluctuations in strong interactions of beauty and charm hadrons are reported using the LHCb detector at the LHC. These studies utilize the semi-leptonic decays of J/psi mesons, and the differential rates for these decays are analyzed as a function of distance between the production vertices. Data from proton-proton collisions at 7 and 13 TeV are used, complemented by data from lead-lead collisions at 5 TeV. Analysis reveals that beauty hadrons exhibit the farthest average decay distance among measured particles. The LHCb detector's sensitivity to track curvature allows it to analyze decay distances of up to 3 mm, nearly an order of magnitude farther than previous studies. The results are compared with theoretical predictions for long-distance interactions of beauty and charm quarks.

Our approach employs topological methods to quantify the encoding of information within a spatial framework. Specifically, we aim to explore how persistent homology can be used to measure the overlap or segregation of color groups in a two-dimensional setting. This research has real-world implications for understanding the diffusion of information and can be applied to various fields that involve the transmission of values. We can represent a spatial framework as a weighted graph, with our encoding/ decoding space defined as a weighted graph where the weights indicate the distance between different color groups. We can analyze this framework using a metric that measures the distance between the center points of different color groups. This metric is converted into a simpler form and encoded into a simplicial complex using a k-nearest neighbor approach, allowing for the application of topological methods. We can use persistent homology to explore how the structure of the color groups changes over time and encode this information into a Laplace operator for use in graph-based analysis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a simple test case and examine the correlation between our topological results and conventional metrics.

This research examines the performance of massive MIMO in dense urban settings with numerous users and antennas, where we analyzed the impact of power control and its approximation by the BS. Key findings include that suboptimal binary power control compares favorably to optimal power control in extensive interference environments and that the BS's channel estimate serves as a suitable approximation for the true channel in the context of large systems. These insights informed the development of a compact framework for system design, encompassing key parameters including the number of users, antennas, and transmission power. By optimizing these parameters, we established that the optimal configuration involves balancing the trade-off between spectral efficiency, energy consumption, and hardware costs. Additionally, we investigated the potential gains from pilot extensions and adaptive phase and amplitude precoding.

A proposed a straightforward probabilistic approach to modelling the interaction of financial accounts during the auditing process. In this study, a more comprehensive model incorporating Dempster-Shafer mass functions is developed to account for the uncertainties associated with individual accounts and their potential discrepancies. We present a novel algorithm based on the generalized Dempster-Shafer method to calculate the joint beliefs from detailed transaction analyses. Furthermore, a numerical example is used to demonstrate the efficacy of this model and illustrate its potential applications in practical auditing scenarios.

Simulating independently and positively regression point processes, particularly those with multiple factors, remains a complex problem due to the limited availability of suitable conditioning kernels. Recent years have seen the introduction of several methods for independently and positively spatially ranked point process simulation. In this research, we introduce the Acceptance Rejection Stitching approach for independently and positively ranked point process simulation in a specific scenario. Our proposed method performs well even with moderate computational resources and efficiently uses given conditioning kernels. Additionally, we provide a general methodology for creating acceptance rejection algorithms suitable for independently and positively ranked point process simulation. Interestingly, when applied to independently and positively spatially ranked point process simulation, our Acceptance Rejection Stitching approach often outperforms previously developed methods that use thinning techniques.

The Generalized Uncertainty Principle (\GUP) gives rise to a distorted space and deformed algebra, resulting in the emergence of the deformed Galilean transformations. Although both \GUP and the distorted transformations have been previously explored in context of quantum gravity, their implications have not been extensively analyzed. In contrast, this paper offers a thorough examination of the consequences of the distorted transformations within the framework of \GUP. A fundamental discovery made here is that the distorted transformations retain the same form as traditional Galilean transformations but with altered coefficients, representing a notable simplification. Additionally, this paper establishes that the deformed Galilean transformations, analogous to the Lorentz transformations, do not convey spacetime information to future observers, leading to the intriguing potential for a quantum-based restoration of Galilean invariance, even in the presence of quantum gravity effects.

This letter investigates the competitive adaptability of the Price's multiplicative fairness algorithm in scheduling multitasking environments. We consider a single-processing node that serves multiple clients with varying demands. Each demand is represented by a Poisson process and requires transmission of a type-A or type-B packet, which varies in transmission times. We initially analyze the expected transfer times for type-A and type-B packets, then establish a geometric relationship between the packet types and their expected transfer times. We employ this relationship, along with sublinear regret bounds, to investigate the fairness algorithms' performance in scenarios with type-A and type-B packet combinations. We demonstrate that Price's algorithm achieves a sublinear regret when packet demands are unbalanced, which varies based on the processing capacity split. We also establish a geometric relationship between the algorithm's regret, the processing capacity split, and the expected transfer times of the packet demands.

This research outlines a versatile and efficient method for adjusting robotic legs to account for soft ground when following precise flight trajectories. Our approach enhances stability and tracking by utilizing feedback control, achieving trajectory compliance without the need for prior calculations. It uses a combination of torque control and soft contact rejection to ensure robust landing on soft surfaces. For control purposes, the ground behavior is treated as an elastic system with well-defined characteristics. Testing this method on a 15-doof robotic arm verifies the adaptability of the control strategy to diverse leg configurations. Successful execution of complex hopping movements on different ground conditions, with various mass attachments, demonstrates the potential of this approach in stable active control.

In the update process for Concurrent Transmissions (CT) firmware, the main concerns are the scalability and reliability of deliveries in massive IoT systems. Although CT was initially developed to enhance transmission rates, its integration with existing updating mechanisms has been hindered due to the lack of a suitable framework. Our proposed DArT protocol aims to combine CT with reliable delivery through a joint approach, where we utilize network slicing and concurrent transmission to increase update efficiency. Our approach creates separate update streams for individual devices and uses reliable in-plane communication within each stream to ensure error-free delivery. Outside the designated plane, we employ plane-switching mechanisms for seamless streaming. The implementation of CT in combination with a reliable updating mechanism significantly boosts the efficiency of updates in massive IoT systems. Our experimental results demonstrate that DArT exhibits an improvement of several orders of magnitude in update latency and throughput compared to conventional methods, while also enhancing the update success rate by nearly 100%.

We thoroughly investigate the relationship between heat conductivity and the boundary conductance of certain one-dimensional systems that experience a thermal phase transition when exposed to a random potential. By solving the asymptotic Anderson model, which simplifies this investigation, we demonstrate that the boundary conductance and heat conductivity share a common scaling behavior, captured through a single fractal dimension. This dimension arises from the potential's self-energy, which we compute exactly, and increases as the system transitions from a thermal phase to a localized state, where it reaches a finite value. This finding resolves contradictions in prior research, clarifying how the system's transport characteristics change upon introducing insulating impurities. Additionally, we present a simplified method for finding the lanthanide series' 5s$^2$ electron screening lengths, which involves no approximations.

In this research, we address the Multiple Targets problem within subgraph detection, an essential task in various fields like computer vision and social network analysis. Our focus is on developing fast and efficient algorithms for this problem to find all densely connected components in a given graph. We propose the kBM-DP+, a novel tree algorithm, which builds upon existing methods for collision-free targeting and features a streamlined approach to targeting and collision-free targeting fusion. Notably, our algorithm optimizes computation by breaking down targeting and collision-free targeting costs, significantly reducing memory consumption and time complexity, particularly in situations with high targeting and collision-free targeting costs. We evaluated the efficacy of our algorithm through experiments and analyzed its performance under various parameter adjustments, examining factors like the number of samples, predefined targets, and available memory.

Our research explores the presence of adversarial examples in quantum classifiers by modifying the training process to incorporate small errors in quantum gate applications, and by experimenting with varying levels of noise during classification. Adversarial examples are created by introducing misaligned angles of rotation in quantum states or intentionally adding disturbance to the measurement process, which can affect the quantum classifier's prediction. To quantify the effect of these adverse interventions, we employ a metric called adversarial robustness, measured by the ratio of correct to adversarial misclassification rates. Our experiments, conducted on a radial basis function classifier on Gaussian boson distributions, reveal that small changes in the measurement process can significantly impact the classifier's accuracy, with some deviations resulting in adversarial examples that contradict the classifier's initial predictions. Our investigation also sheds light on the symmetry inherent in the classification process, which allows for the detection of adversarial examples through multiple independent measurements. Moreover, we find that the robustness of the classifier, as evidenced by its resistance to varied adversarial examples, is highest when the quantum classifier is in a mixed state. These findings have implications for the design of future quantum classifiers, suggesting the incorporation of randomized quantum circuits to enhance robustness and classification accuracy.

We analyze how the $l$th Steklov eigenvalue of a spherical domain responds to changes in its volume and radius. Our analysis, specifically for spherical domains, reveals that when $l$ is a square number, the eigenvalue behaves in a particular manner in relation to the domain's volume and radius. This is contrasted with what is observed in a recent study by Guttman et al., who investigated the same concept for a particular type of domain and found a different behavior. Moreover, our findings for all types of integer values for $l$ suggest that there are domains of a particular shape, which we term "zonal elements," that enable precise manipulation of their Steklov eigenvalues, particularly their $l$th eigenvalue, through adjustments in both the domain's volume and radius, even when that radius diminishes towards zero.

Thees, Erwig (2017) introduced infix and postfix alignment as a means to visualize process nets' synchronisation. This paper treats such alignments as a digital form of art and addresses three essential challenges: representing the underlying graph, choosing the most relevant sub-spaces for interpretation, and automatically extracting the most meaningful parts of the overall picture. Furthermore, the paper describes a tool that integrates these solutions and applies them to various examples.

To enhance radio propagation modeling, deep convolutional neural networks (DCNN) can
be trained with experimental data, increasing accuracy compared to conventional
models such as the Okumura-Hata and Walfish and Samson models. These DCNN-based
models are independent of geographic data and account for various influences on
signal strength, including terrain features and construction materials. For the DCNN
training process, a large dataset of 2D maps and related information is necessary,
making it a computationally intensive task that can be efficiently achieved using
Google Cloud's computing capabilities. This project leverages the Google Cloud Compute
Engine, Google Cloud Storage, and the Google Cloud Dataflow service to demonstrate
the value of cloud computing in processing and analyzing large datasets.

Validating the correct output of temporal planning systems is a critical yet complex task that necessitates addressing the entire mitigation phase in models such as MAX-SAT, while also considering time constraints and unfolding depth limitations in systems utilizing temporal roadmaps. Currently, there isn't a widely adopted or standardized approach for achieving this validation within the planning community. Consequently, available temporal planning systems often lack built-in capabilities for verifying the integrity of the generated models, leaving room for potential errors and inaccuracies, especially during the expansive model search phase for constraint propagation or when processing complex temporal queries in temporal roadmaps. Existing automated validation tools are mostly confined to specific application domains or research frameworks, suggesting a need for a more cross-domain solution applicable to various temporal planning systems. We present a general validation algorithm tailored for temporal models, designed to operate independently and provide exhaustive error checks for a range of planning systems and domains. Furthermore, we introduce an error visualization tool to facilitate troubleshooting and enhance the effectiveness of temporal planning systems. Moreover, our validation algorithm offers performance improvements over the conventional approach used in the planning community, demonstrating complementary benefits when combined with the standard method.

The current methodology relying on static security robust optimization neglects temporal resolution, leading to inadequate cost efficiency and inefficiencies in management. Our proposed approach integrates long-term expansion planning and day-ahead scheduling with robustness against uncertain power loads, however, does not currently model preventive maintenance. To streamline this complex problem, we split it into two separate security-constrained stockel-based robust optimization issues, leveraging Lagrange multipliers for efficient cost evaluation. Our results indicate that neglecting temporal resolution in robust optimization increases costs, notably for power generation capacities; consequently, enhancing temporal resolution decreases the total system costs. Furthermore, our approach confirms the pre-existing notion that a single bold robust solution tends to outperform more conservative feasible solutions with significantly reduced costs.

For the multi-dimensional ionic Vlasov-Poisson models, we establish the long-term existence of strong solutions under general boundary conditions including Dirichlet, Neumann, and mixed types for the Poisson equations. Furthermore, for the linearized Vlasov equations, we allow for polynomial decay and non-periodic boundary conditions, thus extending existing results in this area.

To optimize the efficiency of tasks such as finding relevant code snippets, researchers have applied various forms of graph-based analysis to text. Despite the success of approaches like POSRank and TextRank, there is currently no single method that effectively identifies task-specific relevant terms. To address this, our solution draws on the strengths of both simple and sophisticated methods by leveraging basic concepts associated with each technique. We introduce Enhanced POSRank and present a new algorithm that combines the ability to identify key terms related to a project's functionality with the ability to perform more complex analysis using a basic word association model. We compare our approach to traditional methods in the context of code search and highlight its advantages through the use of empirical data.

This paper presents the findings of experiments and simulations investigating the behavior of suspensions under the combined effects of an acoustic field and a magnetic force. The acoustic field was created using an ultrasound source that caused a variable pressure difference across the system, affecting particle behavior in the larger void spaces. A magnetic force was applied to induce particle alignment, potentially stabilizing the acoustically induced particle agglomeration. Preliminary experiments observed a link between the ultrasound-assisted fluidization and the acoustic intensity, with higher acoustic intensities leading to deeper fluidization. A numerical model was developed to simulate non-magnetic and magneto-acoustic behaviors in the absence of gravitational effects, with the model successfully predicting the shape of the pressure difference and effective viscosity in non-magneto-acoustic flows. A subsequent experiment revealed that increasing acoustic intensity could shift particle agglomeration from a state of extended effective 2D behavior to a state that deviates from the predicted double-well potential model. The experiment also showed that introducing a magnetic force could shift the acoustic-induced transition back to a state that satisfies 2D flow conditions.

This is a simplified summary of how mathematically sound evidence can be gathered to support the Collatz Conjecture. The presented arguments are clear and concise, relying on common mathematical principles found in elementary and secondary school curricula, as well as higher educational math courses. The text also showcases the application of mathematical induction in specific scenarios and proposes unique notations for further exploration. Additionally, it addresses the Tertium non dabit phenomenon in certain special cases of the Collatz sequence and presents a mathematical reasoning that uses set theory.

This research aims to understand how Machine Learning explains its decisions, 
and how they can guide future developments in post-hoc methods during the 
feature selection process. To achieve this, we focus on two tasks: 
classifying German dataset human-resource documents and essays written by students. 
By combining various explainable AI techniques and tools with different evaluation criteria, we determined that LIME's features were reliable and could effectively reduce the complexity of the classification model while maintaining similar accuracy. However, the accuracy of SHAP's features was inconsistent and made decisions harder to understand. In comparison, the TreeExplainer offered more interpretable decisions but was less effective at reducing model complexity. Our findings highlight areas for the development of post-hoc methods to support feature selection through actionable features, improved model understanding, and enhanced trustworthiness.

In non-benevolent networks and markets with multiple stable matchings, we focus on a scenario where consumers and providers are guided by personal preferences and utility optimization. A distinct aspect of this scenario is that stable matchings are influenced by the public ratings given by consumers to providers after a match is formed. To tackle this challenge, we begin by examining a fundamental market structure where a single agent selects a matching by following their self-interest and using ratings from others. Our analysis reveals that stable matchings in such a scenario are also influenced by the ratings given by consumers in a complex, non-linear relationship. Next, we explore a scenario with multiple markets and demonstrate that stable matchings in this scenario can be determined solely by the ratings given by consumers without needing to consider the providers' ratings. Based on these findings, we develop an algorithm to determine stable matchings that are also optimal utility outcomes in a particular order of preference. Due to the computational complexity of this problem, we also create a more practical and efficient algorithm for markets with a single stable matching and provide a theoretical explanation for its performance and accuracy. Human assessment of summary quality, captured in the SUMMeye dataset, demands
 intricate criteria that conventional automated evaluation metrics can't satisfy.
Existing metrics fall short in accounting for the summary's original text and its
diversity. They also show disconnection from human judgments. A novel
evaluation metric, SummScore, is designed to address these shortcomings by
combining alignment, coverage, and diversity factors. With SummScore, there's a
notable improvement in diversity correlation and a more significant alignment with
human scoring, marking its premium over prevalent evaluation methods. SummScore's
outcomes also influence the development of more effective summary generators, ones
that can generate summaries considered better by humans.

We've expanded upon the ideas introduced in 'Compressive sensing for 2-D sparse signal recovery using l1-norm minimization' to develop a sparse recovery algorithm leveraging cross-correlated data. Our previous work successfully recovered highly sparse signals using the l1-norm minimization technique, but this new approach enhances recovery rates by utilizing the additional information present in cross-correlated data. It's observed that our method outperforms traditional l1-norm minimization and related variants, and also that the level of sparsity that can be recovered increases with the amount of cross-correlated data available. Additionally, the method's efficiency and effectiveness are directly proportional to the correlation coefficient of the data, ultimately leading to improved performance.

Recent monocular object detection approaches utilizing BEVFusion have achieved high performance due to their simple architecture and efficient data fusion. Nevertheless, existing solutions are highly susceptible to LiDAR errors and inaccuracies, leading to a significant decrease in performance when encountering even a single false liDAR reading. To mitigate this limitation, we introduce a novel BEVFusion framework that prioritizes liDAR-rgb fusion based on an adaptive confidence metric. This approach involves fusing liDAR and image features based on the confidence of the liDAR output, ensuring that liDAR failures do not contaminate the data used for fusion and detection purposes. As a result, our method demonstrates enhanced mean average precision by 2.9 and 3.5 points respectively when confronted with 10\%, 20\%, and 40\% liDAR failure rates across the nuScenes and Waymo datasets, while maintaining its high performance in clean liDAR environments.

To link microscopic fluid dynamics to macroscopic behavior, fluctuating hydrodynamics uses balance equations that combine deterministic wave patterns, likely derived from Navier-Stokes equations, with random, thermal effects. The article "Link between visited states and long-time properties of a stochastic process" applies this framework to a one-dimensional turbulent flow. The equation developed for this flow incorporates elements from both hydrodynamic regimes. The study focuses on the kinetic energy of the fluid and utilizes numerical simulations to demonstrate that this stochastic model accurately simulates the behavior of turbulence to a good approximation. The article also demonstrates that random fluctuations accelerate the dissipation of energy and cause the kinetic energy to eventually reach a random fluctuation boundary. The study further finds that random fluctuations accelerate the exponential decay of energy and reduce the time it takes for energy to become negligible. The article concludes by examining the relationship between these random fluctuations and the random, thermal effects observed in certain fluid dynamics experiments.

We carry out a new experiment to investigate laser interactions with heated fluids. In this process, a Nd:YAG laser is directed into the heated atmosphere and, under specific temperature conditions, produces a beam breakdown resulting in the formation of a plasma. Observations of the laser's diffraction pattern yield sinusoidal interference patterns, which are analyzed to determine refractive index changes as a function of distance from the heat source. Our results indicate that the heated region exhibits a monofocal non-uniform refractive index distribution, which significantly differs from the previously documented double sinusoidal pattern. Furthermore, the measured temperature variation across the 8mm x 8mm heated area corresponds to approximately 6.5K. Additionally, the study provides an estimate for the accuracy of our measurement technique.

A key benefit of software engineering design research is the ability to provide designers with guidelines for improving their practices. While significant progress has been made in using machine learning for design analysis, most existing studies have focused on a single project, which makes it challenging to provide cross-project recommendations. Furthermore, designers may struggle to apply recommendations due to uncertainty about the results, particularly when design features have changing importance over time. To address these challenges, we have conducted an empirical study to investigate the stability of design conclusions across projects and their applicability to other projects using deep learning techniques. The results of our research demonstrate that (a) deep learning can significantly enhance the stability of design conclusions; and (b) feature selection is a valuable technique for making recommendations more relevant. Additionally, our findings show that deep learning can help overcome the limitations of traditional design mining, which is often project-specific.

In the context of IoT data streaming, the stream processing component plays a pivotal role in managing and analyzing device-generated data streams, which often have velocity, volume, and variability challenges. To address these complexities, the H-STREAM system leverages an advanced, distributed architecture built upon heterogeneous node types. As a key innovation, H-STREAM incorporates an adaptive, multi-objective scheduling strategy at the stream level, which works in tandem with the underlying cluster resource to efficiently allocate processing resources. This systematic evaluation compares H-STREAM to a conventional stream processing platform through simulated experiments, analyzing their scheduling patterns, execution times, energy consumption, and reliability under varying stream loads. Notably, H-STREAM demonstrates improved execution times, lower energy consumption, and enhanced stream output quality, accompanied by a minor increase in execution latency.

The QCD Rratio gamma/gamma-to-u-bar over q-bar-to-gamma-gamma-to-u-bar offers a potential standard model test and a means to measure the coupling constants of vector-like quarks. Studies on the impact of next-to-leading order radiation effects using Rratio data in the low Q2 range are available, yet these calculations have no direct application in determining the theoretical cross-sections necessary for the analysis of detection instruments. Furthermore, research at the leading order has not considered the complete set of QCD diagrams relevant at the next-to-leading order. This work estimates the QCD corrections for the production of vector-like quark pairs via non-resonant diagrams in the response to a photon beam. These non-resonant calculations contribute a substantial fraction to the total QCD corrections in the case of the photon exchange process. By adopting an effective Lagrangian to describe the couplings between vector-like quarks and photons, the calculations provide an approach to quantify the one-loop QCD corrections as a function of the photon's four-momentum transfer. These corrections can then be applied in the estimation of the cross-sections necessary for the design of detection instruments, such as s-channel experiments, that aim to analyze the production of vector-like quark pairs via photon exchange.

The generation of SPARQL queries based on natural language queries using machine learning models has gained significant attention in recent years. A novel model has been proposed that leverages Convolutional Neural Networks and Attention Mechanisms to produce correct SPARQL queries, outperforming existing solutions significantly. However, our investigation reveals that the performance of this model and similar ones can be enhanced by incorporating a copy mechanism into their design. The modified model has also shown improved capabilities in handling data resources with an increased range of logical operators.

To identify pivotal research outlets and evaluate the progression of fields within Computer Science, we analyzed the content of 19,188 online publications from over 2,600 venues between 1970 and 2016. Leveraging detailed CS subject metadata from DBLP, our analysis focused on 14 major CS subfields, such as artificial intelligence, data mining, and machine learning. By examining the distribution of subject metadata across publications and venues over time, we detected 25 notable CS subject subfields. These subfields were categorized into four broad CS subfields: algorithms, computer science fundamentals, electrical engineering computer science, and software and information systems. Our results illustrate the evolution of specific fields within CS, such as artificial intelligence's surge in the most recent years, and show how other fields have been absorbed into the broader CS subfield of computer science fundamentals. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of subject metadata in understanding scientific progress and the structure of stable CS subfields.

Advanced neural networks have become ubiquitous in control systems despite a lack of thorough analysis into their reliability. Previous research into robustness testing has been restricted by the high computational demands of simulation-based methods and the need for large, carefully curated datasets. However, the application of adversarial training and generated adversarial data hold substantial promise for improving robustness verification at reduced costs. This paper presents an innovative framework that integrates techniques from the visual representation learning and synthesization fields to create adversarial examples for the evaluation of robustness in control systems. This framework surpasses existing methods in several key aspects, including the generation of highly plausible adversarial examples through the use of diffusion models, the application of normalized cross-relation metrics for the optimization of adversarial examples, and the exploitation of spatial relationships in images via the application of attention techniques. This framework's effectiveness was demonstrated in a flight control agent trained with adversarial examples that withstood disturbances produced by random noise within an RGB-D image stream.

We derive clustering outcomes from a metric on a set of points, treating the resulting groups as objects in a category and considering their hierarchical structure. Our extension of clustering schemes to categories rectifies a long-standing flaw in single-linkage clustering where adjacent clusters often have disparate cardinalities. Building upon previous work, we apply this approach to functorial clustering schemes and show that adding an extra component can mitigate the "chaining effect" that occurs when nearby clusters have different sizes. Furthermore, we identify the conditions under which this solution prevents "chain reactions" in more general schemes.

Human motion detection in surveillance videos is a vital component of criminal investigation and terrorist detection. However, the dynamic tensor completion algorithms currently available are not suited to processing surveillance videos containing motion, which makes them impractical for real-time use in similar scenarios. This limitation is due to their need to process data from all video frames simultaneously, leading to increased memory demand and slower processing times. Instead, we propose a novel method called Streaming Tensor Completion that can detect human motion in surveillance videos while being mindful of memory constraints and ensuring real-time performance. This approach leverages a dynamic graph structure that adapts to changing video frames and considers the temporal dependency of tensor elements using temporal tensor factorization. We implement this method using graph protocols and expose the corresponding implementation details. Experimental evaluations on four public datasets reveal that our method boasts exceptional accuracy, surpassing that of comparative methods. Furthermore, these methodological innovations significantly enhance the processing speed and memory efficiency, enabling the handling of large videos without compromise in accuracy.

We establish that Nichols algebras over classical Weyl groups are inherently infinite-dimensional. In the specific case where the Weyl group corresponds to $W(E_8)$, we determine the parameters associated with these Nichols algebras, revealing them to be of a radical type. Furthermore, a classification of the Nichols algebras related to $W(F_4)$ indicates that such algebras are exclusively of radical type when paired with a specific set of parameters. In contrast, Nichols algebras associated with $W(B_3)$ exhibit a mix of radical and general types, whereas those associated with $W(A_1)$ are uniquely of general type.

Inertial wave turbulence theories have largely been untested in the ocean.  Yet,  a recent study by Gazzola et al found evidence to support the occurrence of Kolmogorov-Kraichnan spectrum in a submarine canyon.  This particular canyon exhibits high levels of energy input from the tides.  A comparison with an observational study by Alis et al found that the inertial wave turbulence in the canyon established an equilibrium state.  Nevertheless,  most oceans don't receive external energy inputs and it's unclear whether they exhibit any signs of turbulence.  A calculation suggests that the inertial wave turbulence in spherical geometry tends towards the Kolmogorov-Zakharov spectrum.  A comparison with satellite altitude data of inertial wave activity in the Earth's oceans is currently being investigated.

Graph normalization, an important technique with various applications, is examined with a focus on its fundamental mathematical principles. It's proposed that many graph normalization methods can be broken down into repeated iterations of two types of operations. These operations are closely linked to computing Maximum Weight Independent Sets. A thorough understanding of the properties of such sets allows for a comprehensive analysis of the methods. A novel, non-iterative approach to graph normalization is also developed, building on the mathematical structure of the dual block diagonalization of a block tridiagonal linear combination of graph Laplacians. This process preserves the eigenvalues of the graph, moves the first eigenvector towards the center of the spectrum, and as such normalized the graph, all in a single step.

Researchers studied Landau Level Spontaneous Oscillations in a two-dimensional electron system by applying an electric modulation and a magnetic field to a graphene sample. The experiment utilized a large graphene sheet divided into discrete sections, each having distinct electron and photon velocities due to varying substrate potentials. When an electric current was introduced at a specific bias, it triggered sharp Landau Level transitions and spontaneous oscillations in the system's optical absorption. The underlying mechanism involved the system's natural fluctuations providing an energy boost, allowing non-equilibrium Landau Levels to overcome the role of the magnetic field in constraining their energy states. The researchers observed this phenomenon in multiple Landau Levels and across various electron densities within the sections of their device. Key aspects of the experiment included the distinctive signature patterns in optical absorption, the resonance-like relationships between photon energies and magnetic field strengths, and the varied density of electrons participating in the oscillations, all of which were consistent with theoretical predictions for a system experiencing a significant increase in correlations among its electrons.

Our study of the M dwarf binary CR Dra offers key insights into radio wave propagation at Earth, as well as the interaction between weak magnetic fields and the surrounding plasma. By analyzing VLA data across various frequencies and epochs, we discovered radio wave emissions stemming from the binary system's common envelope and surrounding environment. The radio wave spectrum can be described as thermal in nature, featuring an intensity that rivals Jupiter's at high frequencies and is detectable at frequencies up to 8 GHz, albeit less intense than Jupiter's at lower frequencies. The binary system's radio wave emissions appear to be influenced by plasma variations at an ionospheric layer, as well as by gravitational forces acting on the envelope's inner regions over a span of nearly 3 years. The binary system's radio wave polarization displays a pattern reversed compared to Jupiter, indicating a potential break-through in understanding radio wave emissions fueled by plasma-weak magnetic field interactions.

Our approach, Articulated Neural Rendering, enables the generation of highly realistic 2D images of artificially moving subjects based on their 3D counterparts. In contrast to previous models, our framework generates a 3D neural model of the subject and uses it to create a sequence of 2D images, allowing for the prediction of highly variable and non-periodic movements. By extending the recently proposed Neural Rendering framework with an articulated 3D model, we can produce more natural and human-like motion in our generated animations. Our model outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative and qualitative tests, demonstrating a strong correlation between our 3D and 2D predictions. While our focus has been on the creation of highly realistic artificial personas, our framework can be used to produce realistic representations of various other dynamic objects.

Artificial neural networks can be utilised to generate unpredictable transformations of input data. This method employs variations in random initialization, non-deterministic changes, and data masking to create a diverse array of transformations. Employing these neural networks as a source of synthetic input transformations demonstrates that they effectively mimic the intricate correlations within natural images. However, it appears that human perception of these synthetic images is remarkably different than expected, suggesting a need for unique image manipulations tailored to human perception. This requires the development of novel methods for optimising the parameters of conditional neural networks to produce images that human evaluators find engaging. To facilitate this process, we introduce a screening procedure that evaluates image quality through human feedback, incorporating this into a guided evolutionary development to produce networks capable of generating human-approved image manipulations. Utilizing this approach results in improved performance by leveraging human feedback to overcome the limitations of poor initial models, and incorporating human preferences into the optimisation process yields better results than a fully optimised, but alien-like, version of the same image. Additionally, we provide a case study on the creation of a network that human evaluators believe has generated original artwork.

We investigate Wilson loops within $SL(N,\mathbb{C})$ Chern-Simons theory, specifically focusing on configurations consisting of two fused Wilson loops. The large $N$ limit and one-loop renormalization factorization are key points of study. By using an SU(N) gauge theory dual and fusion matrix aspects, we establish that Wilson loops generate the Askey-Wilson algebra's elements. The theory's gauge invariance is resolved by introducing a dressing phase, which, along with a monopole inserted at the crossing point, perturbing the Wilson loops, reveals an additional SU(N) symmetry. The phase and monopole insertions are found to create cascades of higher SU(N) Wilson loops, shedding light on non-Abelian quantum electrodynamics with U(1) gauge field additions.

Efforts to achieve an exact diagonalization of the three-dimensional S=1 Heisenberg Hamiltonian, involving the systematic construction of a quantum computer circuit, are hindered by a sign problem in low-temperature simulations. By exploring various protocols for mapping three-dimensional spin variables to trimer basis states, this study evaluates their effect on the sign problem. It's found that certain protocols lead to computationally ideal trimer bases at high temperatures, suitable for quantum Monte Carlo simulations, whereas others are preferable at lower temperatures. Additionally, this study examines the inter-protocol relationship and suggests strategies for developing trimer bases with minimal sign problems, even in complex quantum systems.

We evaluated the performance of large language models on zero-shot learning tasks, using datasets in natural language and non-text data. We analyzed how changes in language model parameters, vocabulary size, and architecture affect their performance, noting that improved performance correlates with increased parameter count and larger vocabulary size. The models' capabilities are also influenced by the properties of their embedding spaces, with better performance linked to better data separation within these spaces. Our findings suggest that language models have learned general data representations that enable them to excel in zero-shot learning.

A hypothetical First-Order Phase Transition occurred in the Early Universe, driven by the spontaneous transformation of the Higgs vacuum expectation value, and this process might have been visible in the B-mode polarization angle in the Cosmic Microwave Background, which recent analyses have ruled out through searches for this signal. Although earlier analyses assumed the Standard Model's predictions, a more recent analysis based on the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM) with a first-order phase transition found that it's possible for this signal to be stronger than what's predicted by the Standard Model. I've taken the constraints from these analyses and updated the predictions for a first-order phase transition in the NMSSM, considering how they might be related to a case where the Higgs boson's mass is influenced by the sunlight that illuminates it, an effect known as Higgs exchange during strong first-order phase transitions. I've found that future analyses using data from the LHC, which searches for decays of the Higgs boson into Z-pair, have made some of the earlier predictions less likely, particularly those that predicted large effects, an effect that's similar to how the B-mode polarization angle was influenced in the early stages of the Universe. I've also found that future analyses using data from the LHC, which searches for decays of the Higgs boson into Z-pair, have made some of the earlier predictions less likely, particularly those that predicted large effects, an effect that's similar

The Atacama Large Millimetre/submillimetre Array is a 12-meter telescope capable of detecting subtle signs of interstellar gas and dust in galaxies across the vast expanse of the cosmos. Its state-of-the-art design enables the detection of even the slightest variations in polarized light, allowing scientists to study the magnetic fields within galaxies at incredible distances. By focusing on a subset of a vast cosmic survey, researchers were able to identify robust signatures of distant galaxies through ALMA's polarimetric capabilities and analyze their orientation relative to their central stars. The study revealed a striking pattern where these galaxies at a specific redshift range spun around their stars in a uniform manner, resembling a whirlwind motion. The study's findings were then compared to simulated models of galaxy evolution, which provided insight into the formation of these galaxies and the possible origins of their uniform behavior. The study's results, combined with those of a similar project studied by Hoang et al., suggest that a cosmic "barrelroll" effect is real and provides a unique window into the formation of galaxies during the early universe.

Theoretical  spin-1 neutrino models based on the projective symmetric group have been established to exhibit a previously identified Dirac spin liquid phase. This study provides a new direction by theorizing that the low-lying, single creation operator excitations from the vacuum state function as "monopoles" within the model. The investigation demonstrates the unique properties of these monopoles and shows that they are closely connected to the emergence of a Dirac spin liquid. It is also shown that the Dirac spin liquid can be viewed as generated through the application, as well as the removal, of pairs of these monopoles from the vacuum state. This work offers a new understanding and a fresh perspective on the Dirac spin liquid within the context of theoretical  spin-1 neutrino models based on the projective symmetric group.

We investigate an exotic $Z_3$-related quantum symmetry in the $Z_3$-clock chain. This chain, made of $N$ clocks that can take on $Z_3$ values, is studied using the matrix product state algorithm with a two-dimensional $Z_2$ lattice of $\chi$ complexity, combined with a single clock system. Our analysis focuses on the fundamental breaking of the $Z_3$ symmetry caused by a single clock's dynamics and how it increases as the number of $Z_3$ temporal lattice sites grows. We also look at the relationship between the largest Wannier bandwidth and the number of sites, investigate the critical exponent of the correlation function near the intermediate point and verify that it matches the exact result of $\ln 2$. Additionally, we verify that the one-dimensional $Z_3$-clock model is in the same universality class as the $Z_3$-clock chain and propose a general stress tensor formulation for the $Z_3$-clock chain.

Manganese-aluminum is an antiferromagnetic compound that, when pressed into a thin layer, exhibits a unique ground state with complex arrangements of opposite magnetic poles across its surface. Researchers studied the properties of an analogous compound, chromium-aluminum, using state-of-the-art methods to study the behavior of the top layer of the material. Their findings revealed that chromium-aluminum displays the same unusual ground state as its manganese counterpart, with further investigation using specialized equipment showing that its magnetic poles switch direction within that top layer. This unique arrangement of magnetic poles is thought to be stable at ordinary temperatures, lasting for at least three years, with the material displaying a high resistance to fatigue with up to 100,000 repeated applications of a magnetic field. Contrasting results from a different manganese-based compound showed that its magnetic poles switch direction only after it had been subjected to at least 10,000 repetitions. These findings strongly suggest that the material made from chromium and aluminum exhibits a unique ground state with the top layer contributing to it directly, with the material displaying a high resistance to fatigue with the repeated applications of a magnetic field. An existing theory that relates to the material made from manganese and aluminum also strongly suggests that the material made from chromium and aluminum exhibits a unique ground state with the top layer of the material contributing to it directly.
