A novel approach for modeling thermal transpiration in rarefied micro-flows has been proposed. This method, inspired by the $\mu$-thermal model, incorporates thermal degree of freedom modulation and transport scattering. It allows the implementation of a single, unified kinetic model suitable for a range of applications including gas separation, cooling, and non-equilibrium processes. To validate this approach, the proposed $\mu$-model was compared with the direct simulation method and Monte Carlo simulation, with results indicating that it could provide a valuable alternative for direct simulation and MCSS when applied to the steady flow of rarefied gases and also could serve as an efficient solution for the non-steady mass flow and heat transfer problems when coupled with an FEM method.

Existing solutions for semantic parsing in a few shots rely heavily on large amounts of labeled data which can be time-consuming and costly to annotate. Our approach makes use of large amounts of unannotated data that are labeled with meanings, bringing few-shot semantic parsing closer to being a scalable task. We achieve this by learning a shared knowledge margin that brings related meanings closer together in space, and then employ a bayesian adaptation technique to tackle the few shot scenario by making an informed selection of the most relevant data points to use as bridge features. This results in significant improvements, particularly for the smallbench and smalltalk datasets where we see gains of 8.8 and 11.3 blue scores. We also show that our results on smalltalk are the best when compared to prior work that also made use of unannotated data, and that our outcomes are positive for the task of semantic parsing in natural language from English menus, yielding the best outcomes when compared to prior work that employed a totally different method.

The following presentation highlights the advancements of two innovative technologies: a sensor known as DMAPS, which is a monolithic active pixel sensor designed to operate at high rates, low temperatures, and with a depleted sensor layer, and another sensor known as LGAD, which is a type of high-resolution silicon detector designed for particle tracking. DMAPS DPD 56 sensor data collected in a test setup will be presented along with data collected during a physics experiment. In addition, several production batches of LGADs, characterized through the measurement of their gain and cutoff frequencies, have been successfully completed. LGADs have also been put through various physical tests with high-energy particles and their performance has been recorded. Moreover, Tender, a prototype tracking device utilizing integrated DMAPS arrays, has also been showcased. This prototype features multiple layers of segmented sensors that are capable of detecting particle tracks in multiple dimensions during high-energy physics experiments. Lastly, a line-up concept for a new particle physics experiment known as the Proton Lead Ion (PbIon) experiment at the Future Circular Collider at CERN will also be presented. This line-up design is planned to integrate tenders and is projected to detect up to 30 layers of sensors along a 20 cm long active edge.

Using the XMM-Newton telescope, researchers carried out an in-depth examination of two previously undiscovered low-power black holes located in the constellation of Corvus. The mass of the primary object within 2XMM J123103.2+110648 exhibits characteristics associated with an extremely young, low-mass active galactic nucleus with a bright intermediate state, marked by substantial X-ray emissions of around 2.4 times 10 to the 42 ergs per second. 2XMM J123651.0+1251, on the other hand, is a low-mass black hole displaying characteristics of some spectral patterns seen in X-ray binaries associated with supernovae.  Both systems exhibit an unexpected lack of emission lines coming from the surrounding gas, which could be due to a significant amount of gas being blocked by the host galaxy's central region.  It is suggested that these systems may have originated from the remnants of massive stars before becoming active galactic nuclei.  It appears that determining the origin of low-mass active galactic nuclei is a complex issue.  It's also found that low-mass active galactic nuclei with properties of an intermediate state are rarely observed and that further research is needed.

Theoretical models indicate that certain early-type stars with magnetic fields may develop magnetospheres formed from disc material that accretes onto the star. It is possible that similar magnetospheres could be detected around B-type magnetic stars in the Magellanic Clouds using the James Webb Space Telescope. To explore this, researchers aimed to find parallel structures between the spectroscopic features observed in the WW Vul type spectra and those detected in the magnetospheres of B-type stars. They analyzed the emission lines typical of WW Vul type spectra and identified a pattern consistent with those found in the magnetospheres of B-type stars. Additionally, certain radial velocity variations in the emission lines could be due to the presence of a disc in the system. If confirmed, this would be the second known example of a magnetosphere surrounding an early-type star in the Magellanic Clouds and the first with a confirmed disc.

The interconnection between oscillator operators in one dimension and the principles of intertwining operators is explored in this research, with the related Intertwining-OSC algebra introduced as a factor-algebra of OSC. Derivations of key properties and examples are provided, and the paper also establishes the natural relationship between Intwist-OSC and the Virasoro algebra. Furthermore, the Interwining-OSC algebra is utilized to construct higher-order Virasoro operators through Intertwinings.

We investigated the correlation between far-infrared and HCN (specifically its high-frequency variants) emissions in extremely low-metallicity galaxies. These galaxies, found in dwarf irregulars with very low iron content, have unusually high star formation rates that are thought to be driven by intense gas flows. Using data from the Herschel and Plateau de Bure Interferometer, we selected 12 galaxies and isolated their emissions. To calculate the star formation rate, we compared total infrared flux to that derived from HCN emissions, finding the latter yielded higher values, potentially due to higher excitation temperatures and/or greater dust opacity in these galaxies. In line with this, a strong HCN-to-H$_2$D+ ratio was observed, indicating dense gas is efficiently converting to stars. Furthermore, a notable HCN-to-infrared flux scalar relation existed, but only when using the HCN-to-H$_2$D+ ratio as a proxy for gas density. These findings are compelling evidence that high star formation rates in low-metallicity galaxies are driven by rapid gas conversions into stars.

We investigate the topological minimal continuous actions of certain groups that
are close to being virtually cyclic yet exhibit distinct characteristics from
their infinite dihedral group counterpart, including a comparison with the
infinite dihedral group itself.

In this research, we explore nontraditional, kernel-based techniques for projecting stochastic differential equations at a specified time $T$. Distinguishing itself from classical methods, such as Galerkin approaches, this method does not first approximate the solution trajectory but instead directly approximates the projection's boundary using a kernel. We demonstrate in a C2 smooth manifold setting that this method is well-defined, has a proof-by-concept convergence that surpasses that of traditional techniques, and, further, that this convergence is realized in practice. We showcase this through a collection of Monte-Carlo simulations. Notably, this method is distinct from Monte-Carlo temporal Dislocation Dynamical programming, a method developed in 'The Monte-Carlo dislocation dynamics of dislocation interactions' that also achieves optimal convergence.

This study introduces a novel approach for observing and analyzing complex, non-hierarchical systems like those found in plant epidemiology, by adapting techniques initially developed for machine learning. A custom-designed observer has been created with the capacity for real-time state estimation in complex models such as the SIS and SIR models, and its effectiveness has been validated through theoretical and simulation-based testing. Crucially, this observer does not require prior knowledge of key parameters, such as infection rates, making it well-suited for dynamic and rapidly changing environments.

This paper introduces a novel method called DEKE, standing for Distilled Knowledge via Enemy Minimax Embedding, to enhance temporal knowledge graph embedding models. These models learn node representations in a low-dimensional space to preserve property-based relationships. However, their efficiency can be improved by eliminating unnecessary node details. Building upon Arkernel Bootstrapping, a distinctive distillation approach that mimics enemy-minimax games, DEKE achieves this by training with an enemy in mind, thus making embeddings more adversarial. Its distillation process involves two stages: first, it trains an Arkernel to prioritize essential node details and eliminate unnecessary ones; second, it uses these distilled details to train the final embeddings. Experimental results on four benchmark datasets show that DEKE outperforms state-of-the-art models in link prediction tasks while reducing the model size substantially, achieving a notable reduction of 65.0% to 75.2% in model parameters compared to existing models, while maintaining similar accuracy levels.

We introduce a novel Kerr-lens mode-locked Yb-doped photonic crystal fiber laser that operates reliably without an intracavity mirror, primarily due to the inherent characteristics of its photonic crystal fiber. This laser features a compact design with a sole optical component providing feedback and we present the distinct features of its construction along with an examination of its mode locking behavior. Moreover, we present a range of data displaying its stable operation including spectra, autocorrelation profiles and a phase space diagram all of which support stable Kerr-lens mode locking. We suggest that Kerr-lens mode locking can be achieved in similar systems provided they exhibit a normal average dispersion and a sufficient nonlinear effect and supported by simulation data.

Asynchronous offline federated learning allows participants to engage in learning processes at their own pace and only transmit modified parameters when the time is advantageous. To address the limitations of partial participation in such processes, we propose cPACT, a communication method that reduces unnecessary data exchange. cPACT accomplishes this through a two-pronged approach involving data compression and partial parameter sharing. By leveraging theoretical bounds and empirical analysis based on a MAML classification model, we demonstrate that our method reduces communication complexity for both the client and the server. The results show that cPACT is beneficial under full and partial participation, with notable improvements under partial participation. The accompanying code can be found on the repository at https://github.com/hjchlee/cPACT.

We investigate the theoretical optics of thin silicon films deposited onto photonic crystal back reflectors.  By analyzing a fully tunable system where both the film and the back reflector have adjustable widths, we identify a narrow range of thicknesses within the second Bragg gap where the silicon absorbs nearly all light that falls upon it, leading to a maximized heating efficiency.  This effect remains effective even after taking into account the effects of fluctuations in the back reflector.  Additionally, we find that the location of this absorption peak is relatively insensitive to variations in the back reflector thickness, making it straightforward to achieve.  This property, combined with a thin target thickness, means that silicon films deployed behind photonic crystals are highly effective heat generators and thus have significant potential in applications including photothermal sensors, nanoscale waveguides for laser-based heating, and photovoltaic devices that utilize hot electrons.

Let $\mathbb{C}$ be the complex plane with its standard atlas, with the Riemannian metric $ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2$, and let $\exp: \mathbb{C}\to \mathbb{C}$ be the exponential map. We find expressions for two functions that are solutions to the Laplace operator $\Delta$ under specific boundary conditions at infinity. These functions are connected to the exponential map's dynamics and have relationships with Szego and Bergman spaces in the complex plane. As a result, we derive a measure for a dynamical box-counting in the complex plane.

This survey provides an introduction to the theory of high-dimensional expanders, 
a theoretical concept relevant to computer science. It presents concepts and 
results from relevant areas, such as operator algebras and theories surrounding complexity.

The dielectric characteristics of GdInO$_{3}$ (indie$_{3}$) have been evaluated because its crystalline structure, featuring discrete O$_{3}$ units and inducing polar distortions when doped with charge carrier defects, holds potential for functional oxide materials. By analyzing B$_{1}$B$_{2}$O$_{4}$-type compounds, researchers have suggested that these materials could exhibit high dielectric constants. This study aimed to confirm GdInO$_{3}$'s dielectric features through experimental methods such as X-ray diffraction, Rietveld refinement, dielectric analysis, and impedance spectroscopy, alongside theoretical investigations using first-principles calculations to explore its electronic properties and ferroelectric behavior when doped with Gd$_{2}$MgO$_{5}$. Results indicated that GdInO$_{3}$ has an inverted NaCl structure, with Gd$^{3+}$ ions arranged in a tetragonal lattice and exhibiting no magnetic ordering. Ferroelectric behavior was predicted when Gd$_{2}$MgO$_{5}$ was doped, with corresponding dielectric features observed experimentally and suggesting that GdInO$_{3}$ could be a versatile material for developing functional oxide systems.

Our proposal has a new method for learning node representations in sparse networks, focusing particularly on those with a low density of connections. This problem is tackled through an innovative matrix concept called the Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM), which is derived from the network and results in easier detection of more intricate network patterns compared to other matrices. Furthermore, representations produced by SNHAM are more detailed and translate more accurately to enhanced performance in downstream applications. These claims are supported by experiments conducted on artificial and real networks, which demonstrate better results for the task of classification when using SNHAM compared to other matrices, leading to significant reductions in prediction error.

In a typical pill activation device, a capillary chamber is filled with a volatile liquid, and when activated, the volatile liquid changes state to gas, creating a propulsive force that moves a pill or capsule out of the chamber. However, this traditional design is often plagued by slow activation times due to the residual volume left in the chamber. To improve the efficiency and speed of the pill activation process, our design innovates with a two-chamber approach: the primary chamber contains the volatile liquid and the secondary chamber is empty. When activated, the volatile liquid turns into gas, creating high pressures and speeding up the pill activation process. Utilizing numerical simulations, our two-chamber design demonstrates a 5-fold increase in the rate of change in pill velocity compared to the standard single-chamber design. Moreover, the accelerated vaporization in the two-chamber design results in earlier mass loss and increased mass loss rates, confirming its superiority over the single-chamber design. As a whole, our two-chamber design holds vast potential for improving pill activation performance and optimizing pill dispensing systems.

To accurately model optical communication signals with polarization-entangled formats, a new approach has been developed, building on a method called the equivalent two-dimensional Gaussian model. This method first determines the linear properties of individual polarizations before analyzing how signals interact nonlinearly. By separating linear and non-linear interactions, it becomes possible to easily modify the model to account for different polarization modes. This model's usefulness was tested for a real-world test signal in an experiment, matching its predictions with simulations using the more basic Gaussian model. This success confirms that the model can reliably simulate complex signal interactions crucial for high-speed optical communication systems, particularly in formats like PAM-N-PAM-4 formats.

Combining multiple images can reveal details absent in a single capture, making image fusion a valuable tool for fire detection and monitoring. Deep learning approaches to image fusion have shown promise, but their effectiveness for fire data remains unverified. To address this gap, we evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art deep learning image fusion techniques alongside conventional methods using a benchmark fire dataset. Our evaluation shows that while some deep learning techniques excel at enhancing fire images, they yield fewer accurate predictions when applied to non-fire data. Consequently, these methods produce numerous false positives. In contrast, conventional methods produce lower rates of false positives while sacrificing some image resolution. Interestingly, selecting fire images with clearer boundaries yields improved performance across the board.

Taking a mental health diagnosis may involve a significant step of consultation, compared to physical diagnoses which often require patients to notify their general physician before undergoing thorough examination.  Considering the sensitive nature of mental health, patients typically start by scheduling an appointment with their general physician rather than undergoing a mental health examination.  As a result of this initial step, doctors often rely on a vital piece of information - how the patient describes their mental state.  Therefore, being able to accurately identify a person's mental health status through social media data such as tweets, has the potential to streamline the diagnosis process.  In our research, we investigated whether diagnosing mental health through social media data can be as reliable as conducting a physical examination, and applied'support vector machine' for the diagnosis.  Our research found that combining social media data with medical records provides the highest level of diagnostic accuracy, reaching up to 85%, suggesting that both types of data are interlinked.  Interestingly, using only social media data results in a relatively high diagnostic accuracy of 65%, and further research could explore the underlying reasons for this outcome by investigating the fundamental differences between physical and mental health symptoms that can be observed on social media rather than in medical records.

To manage the COVID-19 pandemic, lockdowns with varying durations have been implemented worldwide, yet the effectiveness of this strategy depends on the characteristics of the pathogen and the population. The present study focuses on the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic and incorporates a degree of asynchrony in the spread of the virus and the formation of hospital capacity, revealing that hospitals' actions are influenced by the pathogen's characteristics. A fundamental boundary is established to distinguish between continuous and discrete epidemic dynamics, beyond which the latter significantly reduces growth rates and the cumulative death toll compared to sole lockdowns. Although this discrete model introduces non-fermi hyperbolic interactions, it yields simple, intuitive, and analytically tractable outcomes that align with recent experimental results and the current SARS-CoV-2 epidemic data.

The interaction between the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISGMR) and the Isoscalar Giant Quadrupole Resonance (ISGQR) heavily influences the energy spectrum of deformed atomic nuclei, causing a prominent mixing effect that must be accounted for in calculations. By incorporating the coupled role of these resonances in the isoscalar channel, researchers can refine their understanding of deformation dynamics in nuclei, particularly in regards to their clumping structure which this corrected analysis affects. This revised study draws upon the "peak-backing-down" trend observed in nuclear physics where higher energy peaks dip below lower energy peaks. As part of this effort, we develop a simplified model that incorporates the coupling of ISGMR and ISGQR and apply it to analyze the structure of deformed nuclei ranging from $^{120}$Te to $^{140}$Ba. Our predictions indicate a noticeable coupling effect that manifests in these nuclei with significant deformations. This revised study offers a more accurate "correlated spectrum" for these nuclei in addition to providing estimated coupling strengths for comparison with experimental data. By adjusting the division of energy states between the ISGMR and ISGQR, we are able to describe the ISGMR peak shift phenomenon along with the dependence of an isoscalar current fluctuation on nuclear deformation characteristics.

This paper explores thestochastic threshold-assisted capture phenomenon in a specific system where a particle on a beam is manipulated by an oscillating wing. This system experiences a "stiction region" where motion is restricted, affecting the particle's dynamics and potential equilibrium positions. To model this behavior accurately, we employ a piecewise diffusion equation incorporating a "stickiness" factor and incorporate distance-based triggers for these changes. Our analysis involves proving the existence of a unique stationary distribution, and we develop a diffusion process that mirrors the system's behavior outside the "stiction region". Combining these elements, we create a two-scale weak solution for the system and verify the convergence of the associated stochastic differential equations to this diffusion process using perturbation techniques.

The ability to execute trades with various characteristics such as cost, volume requirements and time constraints on key market parameters drives market movements and affects how markets operate. This study provides a framework that can be used to model and analyze the behavior of market participants, which in turn can be used to develop strategies for investors. This framework, which is based on an established method for modeling option prices, uses a stochastic process to determine the optimal trading strategy in the presence of various market conditions. This framework can be used to make informed decisions by investors who are influenced by different factors such as the cost, risk and volatility of stocks, which are fundamental market factors. This framework, which is based on an established formula for modeling option prices, uses a stochastic process to determine the optimal trading strategy in the presence of various market conditions. This framework, which is based on an established formula for modeling option prices, provides a general approach for modeling and analyzing the behavior of market conditions and developing strategies for investors. This framework, which is based on an established formula for modeling option prices, provides a formula for modeling option prices.

Understanding user intent is vital for providing personalized experiences and optimizing the performance of recommendation systems, an area of study often addressed under the banner of search query analysis. This research takes a different approach by comparing a more user-friendly method of analyzing search queries, centered around concepts with common meaning, to a more technologically-driven technique that extracts queries for classification, focusing on recommender systems as a whole. By merging the study of concepts and searches, this work aims to offer an understanding of intent comprehension, an area particularly significant in platforms where direct access to content is limited. Two techniques that merge concepts and searches are examined: one that statically links search terms and concepts and another that attempts to predict concept relevance based on machine learning. Both methods are evaluated through experiments on a movie recommendation website, comparing them against a baseline that assesses intent through classification techniques alone. Results indicate that statically linking search terms and concepts, using controlled vocabulary, is sufficient for providing a user-friendly approach to intent comprehension and is therefore a preferred solution, given its simplicity. Conversely, the method that attempts to predict intent comprehension through machine learning, although highly effective, can cause user experience issues if notifications about recommended content are overly frequent. This research suggests that trade-offs can be achieved by combining these two techniques: statically linking intent at system startup, followed by dynamic intent comprehension through machine learning-based prediction of concept relevance for recent queries. This hybrid method proved to provide better user experience while preserving high recommendation accuracy.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation can be simplified into two separate components. The equation is fully integrable and can be expressed as the product of two separate solutions. One solution originates from a Fuchsian ordinary differential equation of order (n+1), with coefficients defined by a specific set. The other solution comes from an asymptotic behavior, requiring a series expansion near the origin. In order for the equation to have a single, holomorphic solution across the entire complex plane, excluding the origin, specific conditions must be met regarding the values of a1, a2, and a3.

We're analyzing a data analysis technique that combines the principles of cateningic inequalities and principal component analysis. This method uses PCA on weighted data sums to recover a-rank matrices from limited information. Our research, however, shows that this technique fails for certain types of a-rank matrices. As a result, we've developed a new version of this method, combining PCA with an additional linear transformation. Our theoretical findings suggest that this modified technique is highly resilient to noise and can efficiently recover complete a-rank matrices, even with much reduced sampling rates compared to other methods. Our experiments support these findings, demonstrating the superior performance of this technique over other methods in high-dimensional data analysis.

Topological phase transitions in systems with spin and parity symmetry often occur when this symmetry is broken, leading to the emergence of fractional boundary states. Notably, systems lacking this spin-parity symmetry can still host fractional boundary states, driven by internal topological factors. A classic example is a helical edge state found in two-dimensional materials lacking spin-parity symmetry. In this discussion, we explore and compare two systems that exhibit internal fractional boundary states: a quantum Ising chain and a photonic crystal slab. The quantum Ising chain is a renowned model for studying magnetism as a quantum phenomenon. When enhanced with a spin-parity symmetry, it exhibits topological phase transitions and protected boundary states. However, when this symmetry is absent, it still displays internal fractional boundary states due to magnetization; these states can be manipulated by applying a magnetic field. Building on this concept from solid-state physics, we identify an analog photonic system, a photonic crystal half-wave plate, that effectively mimics the characteristics of the spin-parity symmetric Ising chain under external magnetic field. The study of internal fractional boundary states in systems without inherent protection offers valuable insights into topological physics, offering novel methods for detection and potential applications in quantum technology.

We've analyzed potential new physics in $B$-meson decays into the $\tau$ lepton and hadronic particles, utilizing a model-independent approach. Our analysis assigns significance ratings to various parameters that assess differences between $b\to c$ and $b\to s$ transitions in electron and $\tau$ leptons. New physics could cause deviations from these processes, making related measurements highly sensitive to such variations. Given data lacks complete information about $\tau$ decays, our analysis focuses on the most relevant hadronic $\tau$ decay channels. Our results cover a range of scenarios up to next-to-leading order in chiral perturbation theory. Current data from Belle II and LHCb experiments places constraints on parameters that differ by factors of 10 to 300 from their standard model predictions. Several combinations of electron and $\tau$ decay channels can detect new physics at levels as low as $10^{-4}$ with 500 $B\to\tau X$ decays, offering significant information compared to the standard model at various levels, especially with large $\tau$ decay channels with branching fractions of up to 0.15. This analysis can serve as a model-independent benchmark for future analyses of $B\to\tau X$ decays with increased data samples.

Our discrete-time network-based control system incorporates an extensible intelligent controller using Bass' algorithm for agent adaptation. Its propagation of information and transformation of signals exhibit characteristics of complex autonomous systems, reminiscent of immune networks. The equilibrium dynamics of the controller emerge from the macro-level properties of its individual components. Furthermore, its online capabilities facilitate the analysis of macro-level phenomena in temporal contexts. The incorporation of Bass' algorithm grants the controller the ability to respond to shifting environmental conditions and agent failures, enhancing the system's stability due to its asynchronous updates, processing delays, and connectivity changes. The controller's applications to the control of complex discrete-time dynamic systems, particularly those characterized by nonlinear interactions, have broad implications in various disciplines.

This study presents a novel framework for combined modality MRI image
dissegation and MRI-based patient matching, classified as critical medical
issues. First, multi-modal MRI images are reconstructed through lowFi and
machine learning-based synthetic imaging techniques. Next, the synthesized
images are utilized for lesion classification, enabling healthcare professionals
to identify patients with high-risk disorders. The proposed framework also
matches MRI scans for surgical planning purposes, where the primary goal is
to pinpoint an MRI scan. The framework's performance in this capacity was
evaluated using MRI classification metrics on validation datasets, resulting in
an AUC of 0.9551 and a dPR of 0.8976 for the lowest quality input dataset.
Furthermore, the framework's accuracy in patient matching was verified using
eye movement analysis during an MRI scanning process and patient matching
metrics on validation datasets, yielding an ocular fixation probability of
0.9374 and an eye movement ratio of 0.8956.

The widespread occurrence of complex networks in diverse fields has catapulted the study of complex networks into a crucial component of multidisciplinary research. Despite numerous complexities and challenges, scientists have managed to develop an extensive array of tools for analyzing complex networks, initially published in various dispersed papers. To facilitate the sharing and accessibility of these tools, we have created a comprehensive toolbox, accessible via an online platform, which includes 72 analytical tools specifically designed for complex networks. Furthermore, our platform also provides users with customizable nodes, templates, and educational materials to assist in the composition of tutorials, as well as a discussion forum for user community support. By presenting this toolbox, we aim to highlight its capabilities and demonstrate its utility in addressing significant inquiries concerning complex networks, thereby paving the way for further advancements in the field of network analysis.

Our research offers an innovative statistical approach to link current ecological patterns with future evolutionary tendencies. We're able to predict these relationships by using data from various sources. We began by creating a quantitative model that simulates genetic changes over a hypothetical 1,000,000 years. This model generates long-term sequences of trait values through continuous random fluctuations. Our research demonstrates that the rate of change in this sequence can be approximated by a linear relationship based on the initial difference in trait values and the sensitivity of temperature and mutation. We've discovered that the sensitivity of temperature is significantly greater than the sensitivity of mutation. With this knowledge, we're able to develop a statistical strategy to forecast long-term evolutionary behavior. Specifically, when predicting the rate of per generation change in a sequence given a vector of trait values and environmental conditions, we're able to make an accurate prediction by taking a weighted average of the rate of change in pure environmental change conditions and pure genetic change conditions. Our research provides a range of theoretical and practical results that contribute to our understanding of the interplay between ecological and evolutionary processes. However, our predictions are often at odds with current scientific knowledge. For example, our predictions for many taxa suggest that there will be little to no anisotropy in future evolutionary patterns. In contrast, contemporary species live primarily in areas where the rate of change is negative in certain directions, implying that they will experience an increased likelihood of negative genetic change in those directions.
