Machine learning models that interpret speech are highly vulnerable to manipulation. This vulnerability can be taken advantage of by an adversary with various levels of knowledge and motivation. In this paper, we explore common forms of attacks on these models including human-generated noise, machine-generated signals that seek to mislead, and tailored attacks specific to individual systems. We also developed a benchmark test to determine the effectiveness of existing machine learning models against different types of attacks. Our analysis indicates that these models perform well against human-generated noise but less consistently against tailored attacks. Furthermore, our research indicates that these attacks can be mounted anonymously and are profitable for adversaries. Our key takeaway is that these models' vulnerabilities need to be addressed as a matter of priority. In response to these findings, we are to propose the first fully public and transparent method for detecting and quantifying the effectiveness of these attacks against speech models. This method involves an AI-powered "adversarial validator" role that can offer advice to researchers and model developers on the relative vulnerability of their models and provide guidance on potential mitigations to prevent and counter these attacks. This role and associated system are to be revealed in detail in the paper.

Arbitrage opportunities arise from the distortions that occur when traders' bid and ask prices differ in Automated Market Makers. In the context of our model, prices are related through a pricing function, allowing for the examination of the surpluses of involved agents under a Wald equilibrium. We analyze a Wald equilibrium that minimizes the total loss, showing how the curvature of the pricing function affects investors' losses and arbitrage possibilities. We also establish a relationship between the Wald equilibrium and a more traditional Walrasian equilibrium. In particular, our model demonstrates that, unlike in traditional models, monetary arbitrage is not a necessary consequence of the Wald equilibrium. Instead, we propose a novel form of arbitrage centered around the pricing function's characteristics, capable of yielding positive outcomes. The empirical significance of our model is further explored through an examination of the cryptocurrency Uniswap platform during 2021, with results indicating that the inferred parameters align with observed outcomes.

A new method effectively addresses the problem of handling missing data by leveraging the E-value concept to quantify the stability of causal conclusions derived from complete data, when applied to incomplete datasets. This approach efficiently handles a broad range of missing data patterns and calculates an E-value bound, representing the maximum deviation when applying the most influential imputation methods. Notably, this bound can be minimized by incorporating additional constraints from the Gizelich inequality. We demonstrate the applicability of these E-values in testing causal hypotheses and select an penalized imputation strategy, featuring the least absolute deviation (LAD) as an effective method. This work not only provides an innovative solution for missing data but also offers a fresh understanding of imputation errors in terms of E-values, offering more precise and transparent conclusions. By applying this approach to a study of factors influencing kidney function, we provide concrete case examples illustrating its effectiveness.

The initial steps have been taken to develop a comprehensive theory integrating $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-algebras and their relationship to noncommutative hypergeometric functions on the $q$-plane. An inductive approach is employed to construct a noncommutative hypergeometric differential equation with specified $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries, categorized into four types based on the symmetries' properties. This construction provides a new aspect of noncommutative hypergeometric functions beyond their already established algebraic properties. The method permits a calculation of the generating function of noncommutative hypergeometric values, along with the characterization of noncommutative hypergeometric modules among highest weight modules for the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-algebras.

The integration of Blockchain technology into Internet of Vehicles (IoV) systems addresses data protection issues by ensuring data integrity and confidentiality. However, current Blockchain-based solutions are hindered by high transaction fees and slow verification rates, which could compromise the performance of IoV systems. To mitigate these drawbacks, this research explores the use of multi-access strategies combined with energy-efficient strategies for managing data on a single public Blockchain platform. The proposed approach minimizes fees and verification delays by coordinating multiple nodes and reducing energy consumption while maintaining the integrity of the public Blockchain. The efficacy of this method is validated through theoretical and simulation-based analyses, focusing on proof-of-work algorithms and the NFT Blockchain platform. The outcomes demonstrate that this approach can substantially decrease transaction fees by up to 99.3% and verification delays by up to 80%, marking a significant improvement in visual quality for large-scale IoV systems.

Using the whole B meson sample, collected by LHCb in 2011, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 7 fb$^{-1}$, the ratio of $D^0$ to $D^+$ production rates has been determined from decays involving strange mesons. This ratio is found to be consistently around 0.136 ± 0.007 % at various $q^2$ values between 1.0 and 8.0 GeV/$c^2$. The source of these rates was a sample enriched in B mesons, obtained through the analysis of specific decay chains, namely B$^{\pm}$ to $D^{0,} \bar{K}^{*\pm}$ and including a transverse momentum spectrum between 2 and 12 GeV/$c$. The study presents an empirical observation of the fragmentation properties of charm and beauty quarks as they enter B mesons. The findings indicate that, when compared to beauty quarks, the fragmentation of charm quarks is increased by approximately 60 %, while that of the strange quark is estimated at around 10 % lower than the fragmentation of the light quark, primarily being associated with the up quark, and accounting for nearly all of the light quark contribution in B meson decays.

A cryogenic microwave laboratory with controlled extremely low temperatures is being developed within an experimental area of considerable size. It's envisioned that the cryogenic chamber, made from a single piece of material, will accommodate various experimental setups including 4K, 77K, and 1K devices, spanning across an impressive 600mm in height, with designated storage for specific stages under liquid helium and dedicated areas for gaseous helium cooling systems. Furthermore, the entire chamber will be equipped with microwave-compatible windows that allow for seamless interaction with enclosed instruments and accommodate diverse microwave power applications up to 26.5 GHz. Leveraging advanced helium gas management and an innovative recirculating system will ensure efficient and efficient variable temperature control within the experimental space. By building upon an established microwave laboratory's infrastructure, this cryogenic facility will offer an adaptable framework for an array of cutting-edge microwave experiments that require unique conditions, thereby providing researchers with unprecedented access to previously unexplored physical states. By creating this cryogenic facility, scientists will gain a unique understanding of novel materials and novel functional properties that emerge at extremely low temperatures and in controlled environments.

Researchers found that Python's crypto libraries, which offer a convenient and easy-to-use design based on common problems they've been modified to address, inadvertently encouraged misuse. Despite their good intentions, these libraries increased the likelihood of security breaches. In a study comparing Python to Java and C, researchers analyzed the impact of crypto API design on potential security threats. The investigation revealed that programmers using libraries with a good design, such as Python's, would misuse it less but still create backdoors. In contrast, developers using less user-friendly libraries, such as C's, would both misuse crypto functions and introduce errors. The research suggests that attempts to prevent security breaches can sometimes have the opposite effect, making way for security vulnerabilities.

The problem of three-dimensional image recovery from a single image has garnered significant attention in the fields of computer vision and graphics due to its extensive real-world applications that involve reconstructing massive data sets of 3D visual elements from single-bit images. While existing methods efficiently recover data of relatively small volumes, they struggle to handle high-resolution and large-volume data sets, such as those found in modern images, due to their excessive memory requirements and long processing times. To address these limitations, we have developed a new memory-efficient algorithm that starts with a coarse estimate of the 3D data, obtained using a novel attention-based approach that utilizes multi-scale deep learning components, and then refines this estimate through iterative optimizations that are based on advanced mathematical optimization techniques. Experimental evaluations of our three-dimensional image recovery algorithm have demonstrated its superior performance when recovering data of various volumes at significantly reduced memory costs and processing times when compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

A new approach for reconstructing subsurface reflection coefficients is developed using an iterative method that combines a sparse denoising technique based on the second-order cone programming with a nonconvex synthesis sparse model. Current methods utilizing cone programming have proven effective in enhancing deep target imaging but are limited due to their reliance on convex optimization. To overcome this limitation and achieve more efficient imaging, a nonconvex synthesis sparse model is adopted. Key aspects of the algorithm include a nonconvex optimization algorithm with the second-order cone programming and a statistically analyzed algorithm for estimating standard deviation. Our results show that this method can produce a minimal number of measurements while also reducing artifacts from noise, resulting in a superior deep target image compared to other methods.

Given a complex polynomial, $T_g(f)(z) = f(z) + f(T_g(z))$, where $T_g$ is a composition operator, it's known that $T_g$ is compact from Bloch space to itself. Now, investigate the compactness of $T_g$ between different Moebius invariant spaces: BMOA and the little fellow. Specifically, explore the relationship between the operator's norm and the polynomial's properties, such as its degree, coefficients, and inverse, as well as the relation to the Moebius invariant space. It's found that $T_g$ is compact from BMOA to BMOA if $1 < p < 2$ for $T_g$ being a contraction in its degree being less than 2017 or in its being inverse, whereas in the little fellow case, it's proven that $T_g$ is compact from BMOA to BMOA if $1 < p < 2$ for $T_g$ being a contraction in its degree being greater than or equal to 3. These results extend previous findings significantly.

We suggest a universal computational strategy for a certain type of parameters in specific types of quantum systems, involving the use of wavefunctions at low energy to calculate properties such as the central charge and the fusion rules. This approach is particularly tested using the example of two systems - a quantum spin chain based on the Ising model and a quantum chain representing the XY model. In both cases, our proposed method is shown to accurately produce the correct data. This technique is based on the idea that at low energy, it is possible to describe the quantum systems through a continuous model. This is in contrast to previous studies where the transitions were described using a discrete model. Additionally, this strategy can be used to determine other properties such as form factors, which could provide a pathway to computing correlation functions in certain types of quantum systems.

Traditional set-valued prediction techniques have been successfully applied to language modeling where "unknown" words can still contribute value to models. Yet, current neural network architectures utilizing a standard softmax output do not effectively incorporate this concept even when encountering unknown words. To integrate set-valued prediction into these neural networks, we modified the output layer to include a candidate set as input and proposed an end-to-end training mechanism to optimize the model. Our approach also developed a variational autoencoder based on a Gaussian mixture model to determine likely candidates for words not in a model's vocabulary. Our experiments with part-of-speech tagging showed that the newly designed model surpasses current state-of-the-art models by a considerable margin, especially for smaller models and unknown words.

Conditions are established for a sequence of non-decreasing, continuous functions to converge uniformly at rates of n^(-d) or n^(-d with a power less than one-half), where the resulting limit function cannot be expressed as the sum of a signed measure and a continuous non-decreasing function. This limit function may, however, be expressed as the limit of a sequence of step functions whose magnitudes converge at a rate n^(-d), which in turn enables the equilibrium prices in sequential equilibrium models to converge at the same rate. This limit function cannot, however, be expressed as the limit of a sequence of functions that converge uniformly at rates other than n^(-d) or n^(-d) with a power less than one-half for any non-transitive sequential equilibrium model.

In smart cities, various advanced monitoring systems provide real-time data on infrastructure such as road conditions, garbage fill levels, and environmental standards. Decision-makers can access this information electronically, enabling the evaluation of proposals to improve urban living through the analysis of historical data and predefined city standards, or "requirements." However, we found that human-specified requirements often lack clarity, leading to misunderstandings in decision-making processes. In this study, we presented a novel method called BACQL, a Bayesian-based algorithm for parsing qualitative logic in urban waste management, successfully meeting the needs of local authorities who prefer specifications to be clear and unambiguous. Our system was tested with actual monitoring data provided by Barcelona's "Smart City" initiative.

To mitigate noise during quantum circuits, researchers use mitigation strategies to determine noiseless energy levels and improve the performance of quantum computing algorithms. This paper evaluates the impact of these schemes on the variational quantum eigensolver approach, focusing specifically on Constrained Optimization Variational Method (COVM) applications - namely, computing matrix inverse and eigenvalue estimates. These applications are crucial in enhancing COVM's efficiency, which is generally challenging due to its limited convergence rate. This study discovers that incorporating mitigation schemes can actually decrease the algorithm's convergence rate - a contrary effect that contrasts existing superconducting quantum processing unit results. Nevertheless, incorporating mitigation might still accelerate the algorithm in certain cases. This paper presents numerical evidence and an explanation, based on quantum processing inaccuracies, for these phenomena. Furthermore, the paper proposes a simple, though highly speculative modification that could restore the beneficial effects of mitigation schemes within the quantum eigensolver approach.

We establish in this study that if a preorder $A$ yields a family of cofinal directed sets $(C_\alpha$ for $\alpha$ in $A)$, then the intersection of the morphisms mapping any two elements of $A$ to a value in $B$ exists and is unique, and it is an element of $\bigvee_{\alpha\in A} C_\alpha$. Additionally, this result holds in a wider range of categories including topoi with supima of chains, n-permutable regular categories, and categories with coproducts of chains. Similar findings apply to the minimum values of these categories.

This study investigates the significant storms that affected the UK and the US in 2013, focusing on their spatial extent. Analyzing satellite and weather data, including wind speed, wave height, and rainfall, an instrument-based measurement is used to determine the initial extreme weather occurrence. The observations reveal similar behavior in wind speed and wave height when conditioned on extreme Metop wind speed, showing decay in extremity over long distances. The findings also indicate a higher correlation between Metop wind speed and US rainfall extremes compared to UK rainfall. The investigation further explores how Metop wind speed influences damage in specific states during the storms, revealing that extreme Metop wind speed can predict damage in US states up to several thousand kilometers, with significant prediction up to around 800 kilometers. The study identifies potential causes for these spatial significant findings, including the potential for Metop wind speed to influence global atmospheric patterns, as seen in prior studies.

Recent advancements in large-scale contrastive pre-training for Visual Language Prediction have led to enhanced text and image semantic connection. However, conventional approaches often face difficulties in identifying objects with intrinsic visual features or those that appear in different poses or contexts. To address this challenge in pre-training, we introduce the Visual-guided Texts approach, which incorporates texts augmented with text-based object descriptions to facilitate image-text correlation. Notably, our method achieves top-notch performance on various benchmarks, including a state-of-the-art performance of 82.1% on the Visual Question Answering task. Further analysis reveals that our approach improves mean Average Precision by 4.3% on the Image Retrieval benchmark, demonstrating more robust image-text matching. Additionally, we demonstrate that our approach can be effectively applied to practical, real-world scenarios through case studies on image tagging and text-based object detection.

In the context of noisy matrix data, the top singular sector estimation problem is addressed under a four-fold noise model. Diverse settings, such as noisy entry and mixed noise, are covered by this model. An adaptive estimator is proposed, which involves shifting the given matrix to align with its singular structure. It is demonstrated that this proposed estimator is both unbiased and rate-optimal when the noise is symmetric. Furthermore, an adaptive weighting scheme is developed to handle asymmetric noise and achieve the same optimal rate of convergence. The findings are illustrated with numerical examples and theoretical proofs, including a key lemmas for boundedness in the Gamma and Beta functions.

Building upon the foundational work of Dwyer and Neumann in stable homotopy theory, Mackey functors have proven to be a pivotal advancement in the field. Similar to derived functors, Mackey functors represent a form of derived version of localizations or extensions in homotopy theory. By incorporating algebraic principles, Mackey functors have facilitated significant advancements in the study of topological Hochschild homotopy algebras as well as enriched monoidal models for algebraic $K$-theory theories. This paper aims to provide an in-depth overview of these advances, including key examples, introductory concepts, and a detailed analysis of examples, with the primary goal of highlighting the Mackey functor approach as a versatile tool in stable homotopy theory.

We establish that for a Noetherian local ring R and an ideal I, the zero submodule of local cohomology with respect to x, where x is a non-zero element of R, directly influences the R-bilinear form associated with the R-algebra R[x]/(x^2 + f_R(x)), where f_R(x) represents the form representing the R-fractional ideal, and therefore, it is closely linked to the R-fractional form invariant under the Galois K[x] algebra K(x)/K, K being the algebraic closure of the field K. This connection further implies that for R being complete discrete valuation ring with uniformizing parameter t, and I being the ideal tR + R, the zero local cohomology module I^B_R(x, R) directly influences the characteristic series of the ring R, and therefore, it is closely linked to the Hilbert-Samuel function of the ring R. This link further implies that for R being complete discrete valuation ring with uniformizing parameter t, and I being the ideal tR + R, the zero local cohomology module I^B_R(x, R) directly influences the characteristic series of the ring R, and therefore, it is closely linked to the power series of the ring R, and therefore, it is closely linked to the analytic power series of the ring R.

When working with deep learning on medical imaging data, a major obstacle often encountered is compatibility issues caused by the complexity and varied formats of these files. To address this problem, a Python library called highdicom aims to provide a simple solution for reading, simulating, and creating DICOM images. This library's design enables seamless integration with Keras-JavaScript, making it an ideal choice for developers working with neural network-based projects involving DICOM data. Highdicom's image creation capabilities, powered by Python's Graphics Toolbox, allow for the generation of synthetic DICOM images based on user-provided specifications. For projects that involve manipulating DICOM data, the library offers a range of tools for image modification and includes support for popular Graphics Toolbox operations. Highdicom's flexible architecture makes it an excellent choice as a DICOM study reader and allows for the easy creation of synthetic images or data batches. To facilitate data sharing, the library also includes a secure image viewer, making it an ideal solution for medical imaging projects.

Although our description of the horizon encodes our complete knowledge of its topology and geometry, the general mechanism by which diffeomorphisms preserve the horizon's properties is still unclear. To address this gap, we investigate how diffeomorphisms maintain the invariance of the horizon structure in regions where inner and outer causal structures diverge towards the horizon. In the process, we also derive a more precise version of the area theorem, which demonstrates that a specific diffeomorphism-induced change in area is determined by the gradient of the Klein-Nishina factor. Furthermore, we verify that such diffeomorphisms in regions where inner and outer causal structures diverge towards the horizon result in the maintenance of the horizon's directional area spectrum. In the context of charged black holes, this insight leads to the conclusion that their area spectrum remains invariant under certain diffeomorphisms, which align with the parameter space of the general solution.

Our study demonstrates that machine learning models trained on whole genome expression data can pinpoint specific regions of the genome associated with distinct cancer types and patient subgroups based on clinical characteristics. Using a DNA classification task and patient clustering exercise in prostate cancer as examples, we investigated how models from diverse fields contribute to "explanation generation." The machine learning methods we examined included tree-based algorithms, neural networks, and system networks. To gain insight into the models' decisions, we employed various methods for feature importance assessment. By examining the variables that these methods identified as influential, we discovered associations with known biological processes, further validating the models' accuracy. The variables that these models identified as significant also showed a high degree of consistency, further confirming the models' reliability. Ultimately, the variables that these models identified as influential could potentially serve as novel biomarkers for clinical use.

From a general spectral representation, a constraint related to the Drude term in conductance is derived for systems with strong electron-electron interaction. This property is applied to Anderson model discretely presented, yielding an inequality involving the bandwidth. In the case where the model transitions from an insulator to a conductor, spectral weight'sum rules' are found to break down. This discovery reinforces that strong correlation models rely on a breakdown of Fermi liquid'sum rules' for this transition. Furthermore, the inequality, by linking the disorder strength to the system's bandwidth, provides a clear criterion for this transition. In the case of systems with hopping confined to the plane and lattice-confinement-induced metal-insulator transitions, our criterion matches the findings of prior research. This criterion also predicts that the point where interactions dominate should occur at a disorder strength beyond which the system transitions from an insulator to a conductor.

A novel class of integrators, denoted as collective Lie-Poisson integrators, has been developed to maintain coadjoint orbits and Casimirs in Hamiltonian systems. These integrators leverage specific types of flows on coadjoint orbits to provide exact solutions to Hamiltonian equations, preserving key invariants. As an exemplary application, a collective Lie-Poisson integrator has been derived for a nonlinear Hamiltonian featuring a symplectic coadjoint orbit, yielding an exact quantizer that precisely calculates expectation values without approximation.

Despite the growing significance of discovered planets, previous planet discoveries at early stages of the microlensing events have an unusually high ratio of planets to their host stars. This imbalance might be addressed more effectively by integrating an automated algorithm to distinguish between planetary and stellar perturbations at the beginning of these events. This algorithm is put to the test to see if it can recover known planets in a controlled environment and to determine its effectiveness in discovering planets relative to the current method of finding them in the middle of microlensing events. This study models and simulates typical microlensing events to develop this automated algorithm which will be used to determine the presence of a planet in a lensing event, leading to about 80% accuracy, significantly higher than the current mid-scheme method which has a much lower accuracy for discovering planets, especially those less massive. Using simulated data, this algorithm is used to determine how changing mass ratios affect its ability to detect planets. This study finds that its overall accuracy remains the same, but detects planets with lower mass ratios, which could lead to discovering more terrestrial planets in the future. This algorithm will be applied to the Gravitational lensing Early Warning System to identify planets in upcoming microlensing events and their corresponding host stars, with a predicted increase in detecting planets with a mass ratio of $10^{-4}$ by about 5 times when compared to mid-scheme method.

We create an explicit out-of-time approximation technique for a broad group of conservation laws, extending earlier implicit out-of-time schemes to the explicit form. Specifically for one-dimensional conservation laws with $q$-quasiconvex fluxes, this method breaks down nonlinear discontinuities in a non-local nonlinear batch-like approach and provides a quantitative proof for its convergence. Moreover, this technique can be adapted to higher dimensions and even to the Grad-Shafranov equation in an extended functional manifold.

The connection between artificial intelligence and banking has become increasingly significant as a result of the financial crisis's severity. Predicting defaults accurately has been critical for creating precise risk assessments and internal capital standards. This study examines the potential of machine learning algorithms to forecast non-performing loans in a Brazilian bank, using balance sheet data. Among the models tested, including SVM, random forest, gradient boosting, and logistic regression, gradient boosting exhibited exceptional performance, achieving an AUC of 0.9209. Compared to traditional statistical models, machine learning models showed a substantial boost, specifically up to 76.8% in terms of the ROC curve's highest value. In terms of resource utilization, machine learning models outperformed their competitors, consuming 11 seconds less to execute. This study aims to understand the convergence of finance and artificial intelligence. Furthermore, it is hoped that its findings and proposed model will motivate future studies to develop predictive models of default.

Recent studies on $u$-operators have discovered a connection between $u$-operated versions of chromatic symmetric functions and both $q$-hit numbers and elementary symmetric functions. This research explores further $u$-operator generalizations for $q$-analogs of other significant functionals. We identify two key $q$-analogs of functionals - $q$-analogs of chromatic symmetric functions and the homogenous quasisymmetric functions, demonstrating that both are adequately represented by $u$-operated versions in the standard $S_n$-orbit sense. Furthermore, we establish the limiting cases where our $u$-operated versions of $q$-CSF simplify to Hall's $q$-hit numbers and provide a new interpretation of $q$-hit numbers as the $u$-operated versions of both quasisymmetric functions and the complete homogeneous quasisymmetric functions. This research also investigates concepts of $q$-Hall numbers and related operations while examining connections to $q$-Catalan numbers and the $q$-version of the Frobenius formula.

This research introduces Landmark Gabor Filters, a novel approach to Gabor filtering that produces more resilient image representations against changes in orientation. Contrasting traditional Gabor filters, LGFs utilize distinct central elements, known as landmarks, to evaluate image patterns across various scales and directions consistently. As these landmarks remain unchanged across Gabor scales and directions, they serve as consistent markers, facilitating the evaluation of local patterns and ensemble feature alignment across image orientations. To confirm LGFs' enhanced robustness, experiments were conducted using three datasets, showcasing improved performance compared to existing methods, and further highlighting the benefits of incorporating multiple central elements, namely increased robustness and more nuanced feature representations.

A relative fundamental lemma is derived from the relative trace formula having been established, and its application to calculating and establishing bounds for orbital integrals is presented along with an examination of its implications for gaining access to the geometric cohomology of Shimura varieties through the values of these orbital integrals. Specifically, this result generalizes and enhances the findings of the current approaches by Nguyen Dinh - Phu, and Rapoport, and Emerton, and Sabri. Furthermore, by building upon this result, significant advancements can be made in the study of reduction of stacks, moduli, and Shimura varieties. Constructive examples of the relative fundamental lemma have also been provided in this paper.

In the theory of the reverse matching method, this study puts the RG formalism to use 
in order to get a straightforward expression for the wave function renormalization and 
mass effects caused by heavy quarks having a lighter counterpart up to a specific order.
An application of these findings is made within the scope of the effective theory 
$1+{d}~{+~}{\gamma}$ in order to thoroughly analyze the spectral functions 
$\Pi_{7}{\gamma}{\gamma}$ and $\Pi_{m}{m}{m}$.
It's determined that heavy meson decay widths will be expanded if mass loss occurs to heavy quarks 
and that an absence of quark mass renormalization occurs in the theory, in contrast to what's 
seen with fermions having zero mass. 
Additionally, this analysis produces a non-perturbative value for the $\Lambda_{QCD}$ parameter 
within the standard theory $1+{d}$ in the momentum space with the help of soft mass treatment.

A graph G is k-edge-colorable if it can be colored with k distinct edges, and this property also extends to the k^{2}-edge-colorability of a graph, where G's, if the difference between the largest and smallest degree of G's vertices is not more than 1. Also, if the difference between the largest and smallest degree of G's vertices is not more than 1 and for every subset of its vertices having a size of k or larger, the sum of their degrees does not exceed 2k, then G is also (k^{2}+1)-edge-colorable.

The relationships between weighted Bergman spaces in the unit disk are studied in terms of standard spaces and norms that factor into the $L^p$ norm of their components. Certain spaces and norms within this framework have previously been defined by other names, while others constitute newly introduced concepts. These newly introduced concepts reveal novel insights into the properties of these spaces, including their intrinsic nature, scaling characteristics and Fréchet invariance under transformations of the unit disk. In addition, we establish a meaningful linkage between these spaces and the Drury-Aronson norm, a metric used to measure a function's unique characteristics with respect to its image. This association highlights notable distinctions between functions belonging to certain spaces with weights that exhibit unique properties. Specifically, functions within these spaces with a certain kind of admissibility with respect to a certain mathematical object exhibit uniform boundedness and are found to be learned by certain types of low-degree polynomials. In contrast, functions within spaces with non-admissible weights exhibit no such bound and their characteristics increase without limitation as the function values approach zero. This investigation's findings also shed new light on the relationship between the rates at which functions grow within the unit disk's interior and their affinity with certain polynomials.

This study explores the development of transparent and trustworthy AI models for medical diagnosis. Initially, a unified model is created for multiple purposes, but it faces issues of lack of clinical data and reduced accuracy compared to specialist models. To address these problems, the model is modified to incorporate both clinical and radiological data. As a result, the model becomes more sensitive to its individual components and achieves high combined accuracy. With the addition of clinical data, the model becomes clinical data-dependent, yet it remains unreliable without radiological information. Furthermore, the model's reliability increases when provided with both clinical and radiological data, demonstrating improved accuracy and sensitivity in diagnosing COVID-19, pneumonia, and lung cancer. The model's potential is also evaluated by replacing the original classifier with deep networks, including ResNet50, Vit, and MixOfExperts, achieving state-of-the-art results on the COVID-19, NSCLC, and LUNA datasets.

This research focuses on the economic efficiency of low-earth mega-satellite systems, addressing concerns around interference and orbital collisions that result in debris that lingers in space. To mitigate these issues, the proposed solution advocates for optimal ground station placement, closely mirroring the distribution of users, and for maximizing the distance between satellites in space to reduce interference. Since these objectives are conflicting, the challenge is to strike a balance between the cost efficiency of user coverage and the reduced risk of collisions. To address this dilemma, the text presents different trade-offs that can be made by operators, and an initial model is put forth to quantify these strategies. Furthermore, the impact of non-operational satellites and equipment failures is also examined, along with ways to optimize the placement of spare systems to enhance overall system resilience.

In mesh generation, a novel framework for quadrilateral mesh generation is proposed, addressing two key challenges: routing internal edges to separate mesh regions. The framework first identifies and extracts simple topological structures within these regions to yield a linearly solvable system for edge routing. Additionally, a salient diagonal of a T-mesh is utilized to yield a straightforward routing method for edges, also resulting in more streamlined quad layouts. Consequently, this enables the efficient linear solving common in mesh generation with proposed quadrilateral elements. To further optimize mesh configurations, localized redistricting of a T-mesh is permitting additional edge routing options, thereby enhancing mesh quality outcomes. The proposed methods' efficacy is validated through various numerical examples.

When data stems from a bivariate normal population, p-values for tests can be easily calculated using tailored functions. However, when data originates from a different distribution, these default functions are not suitable and may lead to inaccurate results. A new approach proposes estimating a correlation coefficient confidence interval by relying on an orthogonal polynomial representation of each sample. This estimated confidence interval is then derived from the maximum and minimum correlation coefficients achievable under the assumption of a normal bivariate distribution, given the sample's mean and variance.

We calculate the $S$-matrix of QNMs for black holes with surface defects. This approach can be applied to various black-hole metrics, including spherically symmetric ones. We use this opportunity to clarify points related to the quantum $S$-matrix, including its relation to in-time causality and its application to bounded systems. We also present a method for computing the $S$-matrix of modes localized on the horizon. This approach can be used to determine the $S$-matrix of any system in which MPOs provide information about their Hamiltonian and spatial separation, for example, in topological systems or those with surface defects. We find a surprisingly simple form for the $S$-matrix of modes localized on the horizon, which is a result that should be known. We apply our approach to various surface defects, including the Fefferman-Hirschmann and a new model, to find their respective $S$-matrices. We compare these results with numerical calculations from the literature, finding agreement in all cases. We then discuss how to use our approach to determine the $S$-matrix of modes localized in the bulk, which is a problem studied in several papers. We apply our approach to a model from [Friedman et al. 2021] to find the $S$-matrix of modes localized in the bulk, which is a time-dependent problem that reveals a key observation about causality in time.

We employ the Vortex Methods technique to investigate the local stability of unstable equilibria in the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes system when subject to point-like feedback controls. The analysis reveals that these localized feedback controls can stabilize unstable equilibria, despite the absence of global stability in two-dimensional hydrodynamic dynamics. Building on this foundation, we develop a feedback control approach for the three-dimensional Euler system aimed at controlling the exponential growth of localized perturbations around an unstable steady state. Specifically, this approach uses an optimized point-like control that minimizes a suitable cost function. The resulting feedback control strategy is then used to reduce the exponential growth of a three-dimensional Euler flow initially satisfying certain regularity conditions and observed near an unstable steady state.

MindDict is a lightweight, cross-platform dictionary application, available in multiple languages, including English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, and Portuguese. It offers definitions, word associations, synonyms, and antonyms, and can be accessed offline. MindDict includes comprehensive dictionaries from Oxford, Merriam-Webster, Cambridge, BBC, and other reputable sources. Users can browse entries, search words, and save favourite entries for easy reference. Additionally, MindDict allows users to edit existing entries or create custom user dictionaries. MindDict is designed with a simple and intuitive user interface, featuring organisational tools like folders, tags, and a powerful search engine. It supports image and audio files, and can also convert text formats including RTF and plain text. MindDict is available in multiple formats, including.mdx, which makes it easily compatible with other Mac applications that support this format such as Ulysses.

A key issue in explainable artificial intelligence (AI) is providing consistent explanations for its solutions. The AI literature largely treats model explanations as a fixed variable, but considers the quality of these explanations a separate entity. However, when it comes to application-driven fields like self-driving cars, this distinction is a concern. In our study, we're looking into the field of recommendation services and the explanations provided by models in fields that are heavily reliant on human input, like education and employment. By understanding the link between the quality of these explanations and the reliability of recommendation models, we can identify potential flaws in fields that are heavily influenced by human input. By developing and refining a statistical model that measures explanation quality, we can identify areas where explanations may not be as reliable as the final recommendations generated by these models. By quantifying the connection between final model outputs and their explanations, we can evaluate the robustness of these models and identify potential points of failure, especially in fields heavily influenced by human input. However, relying on post-hoc explanations may not be enough, as they may not naturally occur in fields without inherent causality. In contrast, learning these explanations within these models may make them more robust. By comparing black-box, gray-box, and white-box approaches, we can identify the potential efficacy of these methods, but ultimately discover their limitations, for a content-based learning method we found it's not natural for these models to talk about how they found a item  to  a specific user.

Installing a thin capping of In$_{0.81}$Ga$_{0.19}$As with a high indium content (0.81) reveals two novel in-gap states within the local density of states of the material. These newly discovered states are located at 0.13 and 0.32 eV above the surface fermi level, which emerges with the introduction of a metal gate in a tunneling process. In contrast, the indium-free capping of In$_{0.48}$Ga$_{0.52}$As shows no such in-gap states. Our findings suggest that using an indium-rich capping layer in high-mobility two-dimensional electron systems may lead to surface scattering that hinders performance or even replicates the behavior of another material with lower mobility. Moreover, the discovered states could serve as markers for studying the dynamic relaxation of the dynamic screening length and the evolution of the electric field near the surface over time.

This research focuses on an unknown but fixed concept class $\mathcal{C}$, with all its concepts having a bounded radius $\rho$. Our goal is to determine whether robust learning can be accomplished without assumptions about the distribution of samples. Without loss of generality, we assume that the distribution is symmetric and that the label is assigned in a manner that does not depend on the input. We will either prove that robust learning is possible without distributional assumptions or that it is impossible. It is known that when the distribution is uniform, robust learning is feasible at radius $\rho$, if and only if it is feasible when the data is randomly drawn from the uniform distribution. Furthermore, when the distribution is symmetric, robust learning is possible at radius $\rho$ if and only if it is possible when the data is randomly drawn from the symmetric distribution. Consequently, when the radius of the query is less than or equal to $\rho$, robust learning can be accomplished without distributional assumptions, whereas if the radius is greater than $\rho$, it cannot.

The FS-2 algorithm, introduced in \cite{genevix2019fast}, deterministically calculates a solution to the Sinkhorn iteration, a widely used iterative method for computing optimal transport. FS-2 achieves faster computational times by replacing the traditional min-max operations in each iteration with conditional min operations. This modification takes advantage of the fact that iterative progress is only made when the min is reached, not when the max is. Our study showcases that, under specific real-world cost functions characterised by $L^1$-norm type metrics, the Sinkhorn iterations progress deterministically, as claimed in \cite{genevix2019fast}, when compared to \cite{cuturi2013sinkhorn}, \cite{genevix2018discretization}, \cite{genevix2019conditional}, providing a fundamental basis for enhancing the efficiency of FS-2 algorithm. This insight is applied to enhance the efficiency of FS-2 algorithm by replacing min-max operations in each iteration with conditional min operations, resulting in improved computational efficiency. This improved algorithm, known as FS-2+, is demonstrated in two applications - a large-scale point cloud registration task and a related machine learning challenge known as PCAN. Our experiments reveal FS-2+ achieves speed-ups of 2 to 4 times faster than FS-2 and is up to 20 times faster than POT. This improved efficiency enables FS-2+ to be applied to complex challenges that previously could not be tackled with

We conducted atmospheric analysis of AU Mic's exoplanet b using the James Webb Space Telescope's MIRI LRC across multiple channels, taking 10 snapshots in the 3.3 micron and 7.3 micron channels. Ten observations were made over a period of 5.5 hours with no significant changes in the white light curve. Our models of thermal emission suggested that AU Mic's exoplanet has a temperature range of 1800K and 2100K with an estimated error of 150K and are best described as atmospheric mass loss rates of 1e11 to 1e14 grams per second. It was discovered that the upper bound of loss rates could be influenced by wind direction and is significantly reduced if the wind is positioned perpendicular to the plane of the spread-narrow plane. During two stellar flares the 2.4 magnitude increase in brightness caused a 1e12 grams per second upper bound for loss rates, indicating reduced atmospheric absorption. Our models also revealed features such as Si4 and C2 that support the presence of high temperature mozaic layers in the atmosphere consistent with previous observations.

Investigating the interaction of relativistic particles with a plasma medium, particularly when energy is dissipated due to internal energy conversion, reveals how a particle experiences friction from emitted radiation. Our study provides a thorough analysis of this process, starting from fundamental principles to derive a quantitative measure of the friction effect. As a result, we find that when energy is lost and transferred to other energy forms within a particle, it causes a medium reaction that leads to a change in the particle's motion, leading to a formation of elongated paths in the particle's movement called wobbly trajectories. This effect increases as particles move more slowly, and it generates additional pressure within the particle due to its irregular shape, and this pressure causes the particle to continue losing energy at an increased rate. We have derived mathematical equations governing this process which take into account how a particle distorts when it is moving within a plasma medium under specific conditions. These conditions include high levels of radiation and the particle's ability to quickly and repeatedly release energy, which are both related to the particle's high charge. We have used these equations to analyze various different situations and to find new mathematical equations that describe the particle's behavior under these conditions. Our study provides critical new insights into how a particle interacts with a plasma medium that aims to simulate the conditions of supernova remnants with the help of computer-based models. Our work may also be applied to other situations where a particle interacts with an environment that causes it to lose energy and to its surroundings, such

The class imbalance problem is widespread and affects various areas of study, primarily due to the uneven distribution of classes resulting in simpler majority class instances. Current techniques aimed at addressing this issue often lead to overfitting in the enhanced minority class instances. To combat this, a novel method employing pre-processing, active learning strategies for undersampling the majority class, and a basal classifier is presented. D2, a versatile framework, allows for integration of different basal classifiers, which can be composed of multiple algorithms. The versatility of the proposed approach is demonstrated through various experiments using several classification datasets, showcasing improved performance compared to state-of-the-art methods for undersampling approaches.

Twenty high-redshift quasars in the far south region of the sky have been found using archival X-Shooter, UVES, and VLT-MASSDHAVA spectra with wide wavelength coverage, enabling the determination of their redshifts based on the presence of multiple emission lines. Six of these quasars have very bright absolute magnitudes exceeding -25 mag, and their locations primarily correspond to the extension of known QSO density structures at $z \simeq 5.8$. The findings bring the total number of QSOs discovered in MASSDHAVA to twenty, and their combined catalog initiates research into the study of CMB polarization measurement at $z \simeq 6$, potentially expanding the dataset by up to fifty objects. The project now seeks to uncover more CMB-detected QSOs in the far south using VLT-MASSDHAVA.

A quantum dot embedded in a superconductor leads to the suppression of Kondo screening when the superconductor's correlation hole is paired with charge transfer to the dot. By analyzing the resulting spin-resolved conductance on the superconductor's surface near a superconducting transition, features from the addition spectrum become apparent, involving multiple-charge states coupled to the quantum dot. In contrast to conventional scanning tunneling spectroscopy, this approach provides insight into the behavior of correlated electrons in superconductors through conductance measurements on a quantum dot acting as a sensor. For a multi-channel quantum dot in contact with a superconductor, interplay between its free and correlated electron states leads to a diverse set of peaks and gaps within the addition spectrum. In a particularly relevant context, we explore CeCoIn5 as a potential host superconductor, investigating how the quantum dot's behavior changes as the f-electrons in the Ce ions interact with the In conduction-band electrons.

We investigate the properties of shock contraction in two-dimensional isentropic magnetohydrodynamics. Although one-dimensional isentropic magnetohydrodynamic shocks exhibit the property that they contract in certain systems, we find that this property does not hold in two-dimensional isentropic magnetohydrodynamics. Specifically, we determine that there exists no potential function for the Hamilton-Jacobi equation associated with geodesic flow on a magnetohydrodynamic shock manifold, indicating that such shocks do not contract in two dimensions.

The objective of perpetual view generation (PVG) is to create an infinite, viewpoint-invariant sequence of an object's views. To address the challenge that neural PVG approaches face in generating views with high confidence, especially for complex scenes, we present a new method. This method employs point cloud completion as a precursor to neural PVG, thereby ensuring that the input object views are complete and accurate. Subsequently, views are generated using prior 3D models. Our approach distinguishes itself from earlier methods through its combination of two proven techniques. As a result, it outperforms previous approaches on all evaluated datasets, as demonstrated in our experiments. Additionally, we conduct a thorough analysis of our method's ability to generate views with high confidence by measuring the entropy of the generated views. Interestingly, we observe that the LiDAR data characteristic of the KITTI dataset results in our method performing an inspection on the 3D models, thereby introducing some inaccuracies in the LiDAR-to-2D image projection when evaluating in the panoramic modality. Consequently, we release an evaluation dataset derived from the KITTY dataset to facilitate research on PVG, as well as the source code for our method, which has been made openly available at https://mathml.tjhsst.edu/pvg.

In control theory, discrete-time models of large-scale complex systems can be
derived using the Koopman operator's spectral advection method, which is shown
here. This approach generates an easily calculable, approximate state transition
matrix for use in model predictive control (MPC) strategies. Two novel MPC
methods are proposed, leveraging the Koopman operator to determine a reduced
state space for the first method and optimize an MPC Lyapunov function using
the second approach. These strategies yield more efficient MPC methods for
high-dimensional and large-scale networks. The methods are demonstrated in a
simulation study, specifically in control problems for two complex spinal cord
models with 13 and 29 neural nodes, comparing their performance to standard
MPC.

A thin film of an Newtonian liquid is studied as it adheres to a long, straight fibre with a slightly irregular surface. Just above a critical threshold, small bumps on the fibre cause the liquid to form droplets through a process that involves a complex interplay between the fibre and the droplets. These droplets, known as "marrow drops," sit on top of each other and make contact with the fibre as well as with one another. By analyzing the forces acting at the junction between a drop and the fibre, and taking into account the slight movements of the drops along the fibre, a comprehensive theoretical framework is developed, which allows for the determination of key parameters including the size of the drops, the gap between them, and the amount of liquid in each drop. These theoretical findings are compared with a specific experimental setup involving a metal fibre immersed in a mixture of water and ethylene glycol.

Established Eulerian methods in fluid dynamics theory are based on the Navier-Stokes equations, yet these equations can also be expressed in Lagrangian form. Research suggests that using Lagrangian coordinates provides novel perspectives on NS equations. Specifically, it enables comparison of Eulerian and Lagrangian metrics, allowing for new insights into fluid rotation and deformation. Our model employs geometric techniques to calculate Lagrangian metrics, deciding whether the Lagrangian system exhibits integrability, thus potentially shedding light on a longstanding question regarding 3D NS equations. Our approach also attributes this integrability to unique properties of an invariant volume in Lagrangian space, a discovery with significant implications for understanding fluid motion in both Eulerian and Lagrangian frameworks. As a result, we derive a test for determining if a solution in the Lagrangian framework describes unique trajectories in fluid motion. Furthermore, our method leads to a crucial corollary: if a solution in the Lagrangian framework is known to be integrable, then that solution is also believed to be unique, effectively addressing the question of whether the 3D NS equations have a single solution.

This study investigates the accuracy of robotic ultrasound-based measurements of thoracic spine angle using three-dimensional images. Scoliosis patients who had previously received spinal surgery via the VELDAS procedure were the subject of this research. A robotic ultrasound device was used to obtain and record the angle of the spine's processes in three different dimensions. These measurements were then compared with radiographic images taken during the surgery. The research found significant discrepancies between the ultrasound-based measurements and those derived from radiographic images regarding the rotation of the spine's processes. However, the measurements showed a high degree of correlation with each other. Moreover, it was observed that the reliability of the measurements did not significantly change even when the magnitude of the spine's process rotation exceeded 20 degrees. The results suggest that robotic ultrasound-based angle measurements may not be reliable enough for determining the angle of the spine's processes when the rotation magnitude exceeds 20 degrees.

This study aims to integrate time-sensitive data into the traditional credit risk assessment process. Current methods often describe time-based data using arbitrary functions, like a linear progression for hazard rates or piecewise linear divisions for duration models. Alternatively, we model duration periods using a Markov process with a state-based approach. This dynamic system captures the evolving nature of credit risk over time by transiting from state to state according to established transition probabilities. As this state-based model can easily accommodate complex duration data, it offers a superior alternative to the conventional methods. In this work, we model default periods in loan portfolios using this state-based approach, underserved by traditional methodologies. Following this, we discuss issues related to the timing of default periods and how they can be addressed using this model. Next, we address the challenge of estimating this model's key parameters, including the frequency of transitions and the likelihood of defaults in different state conditions. To tackle this, we present a novel BFGS optimization algorithm that assembles a unified state-based factor model for both factor loadings and duration models. Finally, we apply this model to a real-world dataset to analyze the differences in transition probabilities between individual loans and the portfolio as a whole. This analysis reveals that the duration of defaults varies across loans with distinct characteristics, offering valuable insights for risk assessment purposes.

This work utilizes a public dataset of Hateful Graecia, provided by Zelensky et al. (2021), in a NLP challenge organized by Shift AI. The challenge's main objective is to distinguish hate speech from non-hateful content, with a secondary goal of identifying the underlying motivation or purpose behind the hateful content. The project's primary focus is to explore both traditional and explainable AI methodologies in tackling these tasks. Initially, we examined nine traditional AI approaches and found that XGBoost, powered by TD-IDF, delivered the top performance across both tasks, achieving 89.3% for detecting hate speech and 65.1% for identifying the motivation. Next, we delved into EAI techniques and applied them to a subset of AI models, including logistic regression, neural networks, and NLP tasks. The application of global importance measures, such as permutation importance, to these models enabled us to pinpoint the most influential features in the dataset. Moreover, by using ELST during training with logistic regression and random Forest, we observed a reduction in overfitting in the models. Additionally, by implementing EXPLAN (Explainable Linear Model Applying Neural) in a linear model, we demonstrated how to derive both global and local explanations for the hateful Graecia dataset.

We've developed a novel MIMO framework that analyzes the MIMO system by separating the incoming data into its individual components and then using each to activate separate neural networks. This activation data, produced by the mixing step, acts as input to the networks and the output acts as data within the networks' latent space. Our focus lies within this latent space where the interconnections between the networks and the mixed input can be better understood through machine learning approaches. Our mixture-based analysis rectifies a critical issue within the MIMO framework - the prevalence of random subnetwork connections that complicate understanding and hinder reproducibility. By examining specific subnetwork connections across different activations, we gain insight into how data flows through the network and uncovers distinct patterns within the data. Our proposed method, implemented within a VGG-16 Net architecture, successfully detects a subnetwork focused on object classification and a subnetwork tailored for face recognition. Furthermore, our mechanism enables thorough investigation of activation data across subnetworks to identify unique, distinct patterns within the data.

Historical document analysis encompasses a range of complex tasks such as text
extraction, translation, and interpretation. A critical challenge in addressing these
tasks is identifying relevant and comprehensive datasets. This research focuses on
linking datasets to their core research domains, enabling efficient identification of
suitable datasets for specific subdomains. A multi-faceted model leveraging
semantic relationships is proposed to encode domains and datasets in a structured
framework. By introducing the concept of "is-a" relationships and intermingling dataset
components, the proposed model captures subtle connections between datasets and
their respective subdomains. This approach demonstrates robust performance in simulating
human evaluations, outshining existing algorithms. Notably, the proposed model effectively
recommends relevant datasets for specific subdomains, such as law, medicine, and linguistics.

This research proposes a new compliant-mode trajectory tracking approach for industrial robots that utilizes the relationship between compliance and damping. While industrial robots' ability to follow precise trajectories is limited, existing solutions often compromise on trajectory complexity. Our method allows for straightforward implementation without additional actuators and can easily handle intricate trajectories by establishing a link between compliance and damping. By introducing a straightforward procedure for calculating modal damping matrices, we can effectively tune compliance and damping levels for each desired trajectory. The resulting tracking error significantly outperforms current best practices in literature, achieving a 75% improvement in performance. The potential of this approach is further demonstrated through a real-world application, showcasing its ability to produce high-quality surfaces in woodworking applications with a single axis activated. By integrating this method, we can enhance the precision of our robots to a level comparable to that of a CNC machine.

Myocardial infarction is a heart condition that can be an initial indicator of other subsequent heart problems. We analyzed a large patient dataset using techniques from the statistical analysis of continuous time, related to Markov processes, to understand connections between different heart conditions over extended periods. We also studied how myocardial infarction influences these transitions. Focusing on how individual characteristics, such as sex and ethnicity, shape long-term heart health patterns, we discovered distinct patterns of subsequent heart issues following a myocardial infarction. We developed an approach to forecast an individual's heart health trajectory based on their characteristics, clinical history, and previous heart problems. This approach allowed for personalized predictions, influenced by a patient's unique profile, clinical long-term record, and specific characteristics associated with known long-term heart health patterns.

We present an enhanced formulation of Becke's scheme to evaluate the integrals of the electronic continuum that occur in the random phase approximation and Casida equations. This revised method builds upon a previously developed approach but utilizes a more direct elimination technique to avoid artificial expansion of the basis, as seen in unigrid methods. By doing so, we minimize artificial artifacts while maintaining a basis of minimal size. We incorporate the improved scheme into a program called orca and initial results indicate that it produces highly accurate charge and excitation energies for a range of systems, showing a negligible difference from the original unigrid method but with a significantly smaller computational cost. We validate the new method with an analysis of the hydrogen molecule-H$_2$ where it yields precise results for the energy spectrum of the $^1\Sigma_g$ $g$ $^1\pi_x$ $f$ state across a broad range of intermolecular distances.

The Metric Dimension problem, a well-established challenge in graph theory, involves identifying the minimum number of witnesses needed to univocally identify any point in a given graph's topology. Initially, researchers classified this problem as tractable (solvable in polynomial time) when parameterized by specific graph parameters such as treedepth. However, new findings contradict this earlier conclusion, revealing that the problem is, in fact, W[1]-hard when parameterized by treedepth. This contradiction is further underscored by the discovery that the problem remains W[1]-hard when parameterized by other broad family parameters such as branch width and treewidth. Despite this challenging conclusion, researchers were able to propose a polynomial-time parameterized constant-factor approximation algorithm for Metric Dimension, applicable to a broad range of family parameters including treedepth, branch width, and treewidth. This groundbreaking algorithm can produce a solution within a factor of 3 relative to the optimal solution for these parameters and was also modified to incorporate vertex deletion parameters like the feedback vertex set number, allowing for a constant-factor approximation with a minimum number of vertex deletions required.

In a directed complete partial order (dcpos) equipped with the Scott topology, the Scott lower and upper topologies are equivalent to convex spaces. However, in certain situations, the topologies of upper and lower spaces differ from the convex space. We explore directed spaces that distinguish the Scott and convex topologies, focusing particularly on compact spaces in this context. We define a subspace to be $\mathpilfeil$-compact if every directed subset that is directedly bounded within the subspace is also closed within the Scott topology. Such subspaces have distinct characteristics - they can be topologically distinct from compact spaces in Scott topologies and may coexist harmoniously with convex subspaces that possess bounded indices, meaning they contain elements above which the directed bounds of any directed subset within the subspace converge in the directed order. We identify a dcpo as being $\mathpilfeil$-convex if its convex structure yields a $\mathpilfeil$-compact space and prove that in certain instances, the presence of $\mathpilfeil$-compact and convex spaces can be mutually exclusive. We define basic index categories, $\mathpilfeil}_{\mathcal C}$ and $B_{\mathcal D}$ within the directed spaces, $\mathcal C$ and $\mathcal D$, and establish a fundamental relationship between the indices and the topologies - in a $\mathpilfeil$-compact dcpo, the indices

In hothouse climates with low-sensitivity radiative feedback, lower atmospheric radiative heating leads to increased cloud cover and precipitation, yet this process is complicated by strong atmospheric instability. To illustrate this, a simplified climate model is examined, where model alpha, incorporating Rayleigh friction, is compared to the standard model beta with gravity waves, both featuring a heating parameter, located in the lower atmosphere, which causes a rapid decrease in potential energy. Both models show that with a small amount of instability, this potential energy decrease triggers overturning motions, destabilizing the system. However, when the models reach equilibrium with stationary waves, the models exhibit a comparable, non-linear relationship between instability and heating parameters, indicating similar behavior in overturning motions, which influence precipitation and cloud cover patterns.

We derive in vitro actions for fundamental and higher-spin extensions of Yang-Mills theory, with quantum group symmetry. In this context, the action for fundamental Yang-Mills is given by $Tr(F^2)$, where $F$ corresponds to the field strength. Similarly, for the fundamental action of the higher-spin extension, it can be expressed as $Tr(F^2) + Tr(F^{3}\otimes\varphi)$, with $\varphi$ representing an irreducible representation of the quantum group $U_q(g)$ associated with Lie algebra $g$ of rank $r$ dimensions. Here, the cross product for tensor products of quantum groups is used, with the higher-spin action obtained by tensoring the fundamental action with the representation $\varphi$.

Deep learning systems' reliance on labeled data can be compromised when used in noise-prone environments, with far-reaching consequences for their performance. This issue is particularly concerning given the high costs associated with manually labeling data. Our paper presents a innovative approach to mitigating this problem by adapting the labeling process. This methodology effectively utilizes Bayesian statistics and ensures that labeled data, both created and existing, are accurate and reliable. By combining robust Bayesian statistics with a robust approach to generating and selecting examples, we are able to develop a highly efficient and effective training mechanism. Our mechanism serves as a powerful tool for deep neural networks, providing significant improvements in scenarios plagued by significant amounts of noisy labels. Our research demonstrates the potential for innovative applications of Bayesian statistics to address pressing machine learning challenges.

It is crucial to establish whether an n-dimensional cube has a "regular" triangular section to solve interpolation problems with "positive influence" properties. This problem has a surprising answer: such a section always exists if interpolation points number at least n+2 and never more than 2n+1; furthermore, constructing such a section is straightforward. As a byproduct, it turns out that points equally spaced in an n-dimensional cube have the desired property, resolving a centuries-old conjecture of Maurolyus. Lastly, a generalised version of this conjecture applies to any n-dimensional cube with appropriately spaced points.

This paper delves into the analysis of a correlated random walk's transition probability matrix. The associated matrix, $\mathbf{A}$, is derived from a matrix $\mathbf{B}$ containing transition probabilities based on given location jumps, $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$. The research focuses on a specific class of symmetric matrices, $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$, including the rotation matrix over a finite field, Diophantine matrices, and the diameter matrix. It is observed that these matrices have both a rank-one structure over a finite field and are positive semidefinite. The research uses this structure to establish a formula for the characteristic polynomial of $\mathbf{A}$, specifically in terms of the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{B}$. This is accompanied by a combinatorial proof. The findings are further expanded upon by considering non-symmetric correlation matrices, $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$.

A new method of termination proof minimization has been proposed, drawing inspiration from established techniques used to optimize logical expressions through clock manipulation. This approach identifies clock optimization potential in termination proof mechanisms and provides strategies for exploiting it. It is demonstrated that complex termination proofs in reward systems can be simplified by introducing a mechanism to restrict access to clocks. The method is illustrated by re-examining a well-documented case study from the Raney sequence, successfully reducing the complexity of its termination proof.

In large Eddy Simulation (LES), the implementation of the skew-symmetric form of the Coriolis term is crucial for maintaining the spirit of LES. Going against the trend of incorporating additional subgrid-scale (SGS) models for surface boundary conditions, we employed a constructed symmetric form of the geometrically underresolved surface boundary condition for walls in LES. In turbulent flows far from equilibrium, the associated LES model modulates momentum exchange at surfaces, aligning with previous studies that highlighted the significance of these mechanisms. Notably, this model's effect mimics the action of small-scale turbulent (universal) processes that establish a balance between the surface providing a sink for kinetic energy and the SGS model being a source of turbulent kinetic energy. Although this concept may not apply to other non-turbulent processes such as surface waves, finned surfaces, and cool-down processes, these scenarios are outside the scope of this study. To test this approach, we performed two numerical simulations: one near-critical, high-Reynolds number Flows and another large-domain, high-Reynolds number LES of turbulent flat-plate boundary layer simulations. Flat-plate boundary layer simulation showed that the new model is efficient in preventing LES grids from becoming "noisy" and improving the simulation's ability to accurately depict the characteristics of the subgrid-scale energy. Furthermore, this approach has inherent mathematical properties which guarantee that the solution has a star-shaped form and meets the requirement of being skew-symmetric. We analyze the gauged baby Skyrme model, specifically a version that incorporates $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry. By making certain transformations, we can simplify the equations and derive a reduced gauge-invariant action. Our main finding is that for certain self-dual gauge fields, the baby Skyrme energy functional reaches its minimum. Furthermore, we categorize stable solitons based on their profiles: vortex, gauged hopfion, and truncated hopfion solitons.

A lattice version of the Weyl semimetal model, incorporating the influence of symmetry and angular momentum, is examined in this work. By applying group theory to a set of symmetry operators, the research identifies the symmetronic structure within the lattice model and a associated Wilson-Chern number that distinguishes between topological and rank-ordering phases, given crystal symmetry. In the event that crystal symmetry is absent, conventional symmetry analysis, as seen in previous studies, applies. Additionally, numerical investigations are performed to determine how the introduction of a symmetry-related anisotropy affects the semimetal's phase, often producing a nearby phase where both 3D Weyl points and a M.A. point in a triangular lattice are present. In such a situation, the semimetal's phase is stabilized by a certain range of parameters. Lastly, possible time-reversal symmetry-breaking terms are added in the lattice model, allowing for the description of a related quantum anomalous Hall insulator, formed when the time-reversal symmetry is broken and resulting in the incorporation of a quantized Wilson-Chern number from one of the Weyl points at the semimetal's boundary order.

A novel nanoantenna design combines a hyperbolic metamaterial (HMM) with a flat metal plate that forms a cavity between the HMM and a ground plane. By using the scattering spectrum of this nanoantenna, we observe an Fano-like resonance within the dark additive medium. With the HMM made of silicon and a plate separated by a silicon dioxide cavity, we observe a prominent resonance at 632.8 nm when illuminated at the wavelength of a standard desktop light source. We demonstrate in simulations that resonances occur due to interactions between various modes of the system. Notably, we find that the positions of resonances can be modified independently by adjusting the thickness of the plate or the cavity, thereby offering control over the phase at different resonances. Our work presents a new method for designing and analyzing HMM-based nanoantennas that provide a methodical approach to understanding their resonance mechanisms and associated optical properties.

Amorphous materials spontaneously form complex network structures lacking elemental order, yet exhibiting impressive resilience and efficiency properties. As a result of their inherent disorder, these materials consistently fail to meet the strict criteria for perfect elastic behavior set by crystalline materials. Instead, crucially impacting their mechanical performance, these materials engage in a vast array of plastic events which essentially constitute a memory loss mechanism, complicating attempts to replicate their behavior in computer simulations and experiments. Despite these challenges, it's now evident that carefully engineered stress concentrations - akin to those found in nature - can serve as potent platforms for harnessing and controlling these plastic events, providing a foundation for developing novel approaches to predicting and crafting materials with optimized mechanical properties.

The band structure of silicene on a substrate has been extensively studied in recent years. A specific theoretical model has been employed to analyze the self-exclusion effect in silicene. By expanding this model to include a Hubbard Hamiltonian, researchers gained insight into the impact of Hubbard parameters. Introducing manganese atoms onto silicene yielded unique Hubbard parameters that varied depending on the manganese's position. A comparison of manganese-decorated silicene's electronic properties with that of a single, isolated manganese atom revealed significant differences. When manganese atoms were placed on the opposite sites of silicene's sublattices, their Hubbard parameters displayed distinct variations. Furthermore, researchers discovered that a specific configuration of manganese atoms would produce four distinct energy bands, including one, two, and one band, respectively. A calculation of the system's ferromagnetic energy revealed the presence of competitive forces between two possible arrangements of manganese atoms, known as A and B configurations.
